speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
maintopic: THE LATE EARL ALEXANDER OF TUNIS
subtopic: EXPRESSION OF REGRET ON PASSING OF FORMER GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure that I speak for all members of this house and for all Canadians when I say how grieved we are this day on receipt of the news of the death of Earl Alexander of Tunis. His close ties with this country and his obvious liking for Canada and for Canadians gave him a special place in the hearts of all of us.
Earl Alexander served as Governor General of Canada from 1945 through 1952. During that period he became familiar to tens of thousands of Canadians who had the good fortune to meet him in his many travels throughout this country. To millions of other Canadians who observed his zest for life, his keen interest in skiing, and the roots which members of his family established in Canada, there evolved an open and sincere friendship and admiration. They responded as warmly to him as did he to Canada.

But it was long before his stay in Canada that Canadians heard of Viscount Alexander, who had earned an exceptional reputation during the war of 1939, as much by his military feats as by his talents as a great strategist. He directed the Dunkirk evacuation in 1940 and was one of the last to leave the beach. Later, in Burma, he headed the Allied forces for two years, during the campaign against the Japanese. Moreover, in 1944-45, as Supreme Commander of the Allied forces in the Mediterranean, he contributed to the victory of the free world; at that time, a motorized brigade and two divisions from Canada were among the troops under his command.

Earl Alexander visited Canada many times following his return to Britain and his assumption of the office of Minister of Defence.
The Honourable the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), the Right Honourable Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and I had the pleasure of travelling with him from Washington to Ottawa only a few weeks ago following the funeral of his old colleague in arms, General Eisenhower. But it is in his role of Governor General that Canadians will remember him best. Then, as host to Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip on their first tour of Canada in 1951, he established new traditions at Government House by introducing his royal guests and the premises to a lively square dance.
Earl Alexander bears another Canadian distinction. He was sworn a member of Her Majesty's Privy Council for Canada.
The passing of Earl Alexander of Tunis will be widely mourned throughout Canada, the Commonwealth and much of the world. He will long be remembered for his human qualities, his inspiring leadership in moments of crisis, his courage, and for the devotion with which he performed his many duties.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, supported by the Leader of the Opposition, to suggest that as a tribute to the memory of this great public servant of his Sovereign, of Canada and of the Commonwealth, and as a mark of our deep sympathy with Lady Alexander, and with all members of Earl Alexander's family, we stand together for a moment of silence and mournful reflection.
{Whereupon the house stood in silence.]

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Transport):
subtopic: TORONTO AND MONTREAL AIRPORT HELICOPTER SERVICE
speechtext:
In so far as the Minister of Transport is concerned: The introduction and operation of helicopter services, like any other commercial air service, has to be licensed by the Canadian Transport Commission upon application by a carrier. This rule applies to Air Canada as well as to other carriers and therefore the corporation's management would have to decide itself on the merits of an	
June 16, 1969

operation before an application would be made. Air Canada informs me that at the present time they have no intention to apply for a licence to provide helicopter services.
The federal government maintains constant surveillance on developments in the helicopter field. Two reports published in 1966 (namely "Scheduled Helicopter Operations in Canada" by the Transportation Policy and Research Branch of the Department of Transport, and "Scheduled Helicopter Operations and their Applicability Within Canada" by the then Air Transport Board) provided a good assessment of the situation as it then existed. Both reports concluded that with existing equipment the introduction of scheduled passenger helicopter services would be premature, mainly due to the very high operating costs of the equipment available.
Nothing has happened in the interval since 1966 to change the situation. Two companies, Dominion Helicopter Ltd. and Pegasus Airlift, provided helicopter services at Expo 67, but I understand that the financial results were not altogether satisfactory. In the U.S., helicopter services have expanded in some areas and are threatened by STOL (short take-off and landing) aircraft in others. However, there are indications that high capacity helicopters may become available in the late 1970's with much lower operating costs; in the meantime, it is expected that traffic will continue its rapid growth. These developments will be watched closely to ensure that prompt and effective action is taken as soon as conditions warrant.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare following up a question I asked last week with reference to the drugs which have been designated by the food and drug administration of the United States as being ineffective or even dangerous to patients. speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of Amateur Sport; Minister of National Health and Welfare
maintopic: RESTRICTIONS TO PREVENT SALES INVOLVING RISK TO PATIENTS
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. I did check with the Food and Drug Directorate this morning in order to reply to the hon. member, and I would advise it is our feeling that the story the hon. member is quoting is erroneous. I should reiterate that this really does not involve a question,- although it is a point,-that affects the safety and health of the individual, but rather a suspicion that there might be claims in respect of some of these drugs which cannot be substantiated.

speechtext:
Notwithstanding the substantial increase in prices, the minister should at least hand out cigars on this occasion to celebrate, if nothing else, the fact that he will now receive the family allowance.
As I said at the outset, this is about the only area in which the minister can be complimented, because the problem highlighted
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers in the resolution now before the house is a very serious one. In a very broad sense it refers to the serious problem of the rising inflation now facing Canada.
There is no shortage of analyses by learned economists, businessmen and bankers, and by ministers in the house, not forgetting speeches by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, which all have one thing in common: They all seem to be pretending with grim determination to get inflation in this country under control. The many articles in leading journals of this country, the speeches of the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the many editorials written by learned financial columnists all pinpoint in a sophisticated and interesting way the serious problem of inflation.
What should be of the utmost importance to this parliament and to this country, Mr. Speaker, is the grim toll that inflation is taking among the average wage earners of Canada and their families. I refer to the working man who is trying adequately to clothe, feed and house his family in this era of rising prices and spiralling inflation, and to the sad prospect of families going deeper and deeper into debt just to provide what some of us consider to be the bare essentials of life.
In analysing the situation it is interesting to note the response of the government to this very serious problem. The government has responded by raising taxes, supposedly to curtail inflation. All one has to do is to examine every budget that has been brought in by this Liberal government since 1965. Then finally in December 1968 the white paper on prices and incomes was published, and it is interesting to note that it recommended another study group to study a matter that has already received a considerable amount of study in this country. I suggest that is a weak response to this very serious matter. It took six months to name the chairman of the commission and we still to this day have not had the other members named. This points to the fact that this commission has yet to get down to work, for how can it start work when it does not yet its full complement of members?
Thousands of people in this country are suffering today from privation of every kind. There is every indication to the house and to the country that notwithstanding the much heralded just society, with all its great promise, thic governement just does not seem to care. There has yet to be an indication from
10160	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers either the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or his colleagues in the government that they view this matter with the gravity it demands. It would appear that the just society is nothing but a hypocrisy, and a shameful hypocrisy at that, because it perpetrates a grave injustice on the working people in Canada who are suffering.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) has made a very useful recommendation in this house, namely that we set up prices and wage guidelines throughout the economy. This suggestion was made with the full understanding that it would not be popularly received either by the business community or by organized labour. Yet it is a constructive suggestion, a suggestion that takes into account the severity of the crisis that we are facing in this country today. Granted, it would be only an interim measure, but at least it would be one measure that would break the vicious stranglehold that inflation has on Canadians today.
It might be worth while to refer briefly to some statistics. Food prices in this country have risen steadily since 1965. In that year there was a rise of 2.4 per cent; in 1966 a rise of 3.7 per cent; in 1967 a rise of 3.5 per cent; in 1968 a rise of 4.1 per cent; and as of March this year the indication is there has been a rise of 2.5 per cent, giving a total increase in the cost of living in this country since 1965 of 13.7 per cent.
If I may break those figures down further, it is interesting to note that one of the biggest increases is in the price of food. The cumulative increase in the price of food since 1965 has been approximately 12.5 per cent. The cost of housing has increased since 1965 by 15.4 per cent. The cost of clothing since 1965 has increased by 14 per cent. As far as the cost of shelter is concerned, since 1968-in just one year-rents have increased by 4.2 per cent; home ownership costs by 8.5 per cent; property taxes by 7.2 per cent mortgage interest by 12.4 per cent repairs to houses by 5.2 per cent; and the cost of new houses by 8.2 per cent.
This is a catalogue of the injustices suffered by the working people of this country, the people for whom this government seems to have no regard. Inflation hurts the economy of the whole country, but it has its most severe impact on the average working people of the country, who can least afford to have their purchasing power eroded in this way. I refer to poor people in general, to those people living on fixed incomes and those who

DEBATES	June 16, 1969
must try to survive on the minimum wages throughout the country. These are the people who are being crippled by inflation. They are being crippled by this government's phony war against inflation.
[DOT] (2:50 p.m.)
It is obvious to all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that the pensioners are the ones who suffer from inflation, because they are the people on the real fixed incomes. They cannot control the rapid decline in their income, as a consequence of inflation, and their actual standard of living. It should appear obvious to all hon. members that the plight of these people is to be deplored.
Pensioners are not the only group directly affected. The ability to avoid the burden of inflation depends on the consumer's ability to get more income. The poor of this country, the people who have been referred to as the other Canada, are indeed limited in that capacity. Generally speaking, they fall outside the trade union movement because they are largely unorganized and collectively inarticulate. They have no one to speak for them, save hon. members of this house. They have no one to champion their cause, not even the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Certainly they have given up hope in the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his just society.
Many of the people I indicated depend upon the minimum wage laws as their only protection. Individual hon. members are familiar with the minimum wage laws in their respective provinces. In my province of Newfoundland, it is $1 an hour for men and 70 cents an hour for women.
Since the last revision of the federal minimum wage laws in 1966, rampant inflation has eroded the value of their protection by over 10 par cent. It is these people we should be concerned about. The pensioners and the poor people are paying the heaviest price for this government's incompetence. Unfortunately this represents too large a proportion of our Canadian society. According to the latest review of the Economic Council of Canada, at least one Canadian in five suffers from poverty. Millions of pensioners must be added to this figure in order to arrive at a realistic consensus of the actual casualty figure.
It appears the minister's sensitivity to the plight of the silent constituency of the poor must be pricked more often by members of parliament, and I hope they will do so in the course of the debate today because hon.

members are their only spokesmen. The suffering poor of Canada are largely invisible. A country as rich as Canada need not and should not tolerate the increasing misery caused for these groups by inflationary price movements, even if that misery is hidden away in old houses, garrets and slums throughout the country. When we think of slums, garrets and inadequate accommodation, we immediately think of rental costs, because the poor of this country have to pay rents. All too often they are exploited by unscrupulous landlords.
Perhaps some statistics should be placed on the record. The consumer price index shows tenant costs have risen by 10.7 per cent from 1966 to March, 1969, with a 4.2 per cent increase between March, 1968 and March, 1969. In one year, Mr. Speaker, there was a 4.2 per cent increase. The Ottawa Real Estate Board reports the following: The present vacancy rate for apartment buildings is about 3 per cent. A 5 per cent vacancy rate would constitute a normal market situation, according to this board. Most of those vacant are of the luxury type with rents running on the average from $170 to $225.
It is a well known statistical fact that most people have to set aside 25 per cent of their income for rental payments in order to have a roof over their heads, but the great majority of the housing available for rent today is of the high priced variety, anywhere from $350 a month upwards. The situation is not expected to improve, since mortgage rates are increasing for the owners and, unfortunately, these increases are being passed along to the tenants by increased rents. The President of the Canadian Association of Real Estate Boards said this:
Sixty per cent of persons seeking homes do not have the income for one at current prices. Since they cannot qualify for C.M.H.C. loans restricting payments to 27 per cent of income they are forced into rental accommodation where many pay up to 40 per cent of their income.
These are the poor, the unrepresented people of this country. The minister knows of an instance, which was given publicity yesterday in a broadcast in which the minister appeared, of a woman and her six children living in this city of Ottawa. This woman is forced to live in two rooms on the third floor without the amenities, and must pay $120 a month rent because there is no public housing in the city of Ottawa available to her.
The Hellyer task force on housing covered this matter very adequately. It is very interesting to note what the former Minister
of Transport found out when he went across the country and visited the slums and ghettos of our cities. He went into the rural blighted areas of this country. He was so deplored and shocked at what he saw that when he came back he said to his colleagues in the government: If you don't do something about it, I cannot in conscience stay on in government. And this is precisely what he did; he resigned. I suggest the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs should take the same exercise upon himself. He should go across this country and talk to the poor people in our cities and rural areas. He can ask them how they manage on their low incomes and rising prices. These people have to pay the same prices as those in the middle and upper income brackets.
They don't manage, Mr. Speaker. If the real truth were known many of them, and especially their children, suffer the consequences of diet deficiencies. This is in Canada in 1969, the first year of the just society. Shame on this government and shame on their so-called just society.

speechtext:
I suspect that if the minister carries on in the way he has been he will not lose his head but will lose his department. The rise in the retail prices of beef across Canada is becoming intolerable to Canadians. The price of sirloin steak last week varied from $1.39 per pound in Vancouver to $1.55 in Montreal, $1.59 in Toronto, $1.69 in seven other major cities, $1.75 in Halifax, and was so high in St. John's, Newfoundland, that nobody could afford to buy it.
Although some claim that the main impetus in the price increases comes from the long overdue price increase to farmers, it is grossly unfair to blame the farmers. The president of the Ontario Farmers Union has pointed out that the price the farmers receive for cattle has increased only about seven cents a pound but that beef prices to the consumer have gone up anywhere from 30 cents to 50 cents a pound. In fact he blames the increase directly on the chain stores. The recent increase in the cost of beef substantiates this point. Yet notwithstanding the pleas that have been made by hon. members in this house, and notwithstanding the resolution passed last week at the meeting of the Canadian Association of Consumers, not to mention numerous other resolutions passed in other parts of the country, the government sits idly by and refuses to investigate the serious and dramatic rise in the cost of beef.

DEBATES	June 16, 1969
Canadian meat packers maintain that they have been operating at a very low profit margin for several years. They claim that they cannot absorb any part of the basic increase in the price of meat without incurring a loss. Consequently they pass on the full increase to the retailer, and it is up to the retailer to adjust his prices accordingly.
But even if the price increase to retailers occurred at an awkward time, just when prices were moving from the winter to the summer pattern, it would be interesting to know why prices at the retail level are higher than those charged by frozen food suppliers. Other hon. members will have a great deal to say about this subject, Mr. Speaker. Some of them represent areas where this problem is of vital concern. Somebody in this country is profiteering, and the minister has the responsibility, under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act, to find out exactly who it is.
In the course of his remarks in the house on June 5 and during a public affairs program on C.B.C. radio the minister said that this was the very essence of a free, competitive, market economy. The minister's philosophy is that if things are too high in price consumers should seek substitutes or alternatives. If this is the philosophy of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, why do we need a Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs? If everything is to be blamed on the law of supply and demand, what is the minister's role?
I suggest, and this is becoming increasingly evident, that the minister has followed in the footsteps of that other former illustrious member of parliament, the former Minister of Transport who built an empire for himself before he left the house. All the Minister of Consumer and Corporate affairs has done is create a department and build his own little empire in the bureaucracy of Canada.
Somebody has just suggested to me that we had a similar example a few years ago when the government set up a new Department of Industry. That department was set up in much the same way as the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It took under its control various functions of government that were being conducted by other departments of government. Then we went the full cycle with the Department of Industry. A few years later the government had to tear the whole thing down, at considerable cost to the taxpayer.
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
The minister is another empire builder. Canadian consumers looked with real hope to the formation of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. They looked to the new minister as their knight on a charger in white and shining armour. All they got was a paper tiger. Some tiger-

speechtext:
And very costly paper. The working men and women of this country continue to suffer from rising prices. They continue to suffer the consequences of every rise in the cost of living index. It is becoming painfully evident that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has neither the power, the ability nor the inclination to do anything about it.
Within the last year or so several studies have raised serious doubts concerning the adequacy of our retail food distribution system. In most cases the reports dealt with practices that were deemed injurious to the interests of Canadian consumers. In most cases the reports issued a clear call for study and action by the federal Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In all cases it appears that the minister and the government have chosen to do nothing to protect the Canadian consumers.
The first of these reports was that of the Royal Commission on Consumer Problems and Inflation, more popularly know as the Batten report. In December, 1963, the governments of the three prairie provinces jointly established this commission, under the chairmanship of Judge Mary Batten, to study the crippling problem of inflation. The commission received 150 submissions from the public and undertook a number of staff studies into specific questions. The report of the commission, which was made public in the spring of 1968, raised severe doubts about whether the consumer interest was being best served by the existing system of retail food distribution. According to the report the grocery industry is deficient on several important accounts. It may be worth noting them here.
The first point made by the report is that the largest sellers have acquired sufficient power to enable prices to rise above competitive levels, thereby earning excess profits for the large chains. The second point it made is that excessive building of stores has led to sub-optimal rates of utilization of stores. The third point is that the position and power of the chains have led to and require the use of
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers self-cancelling and costly advertising campaigns.
The commission made several recommendations which were of direct relevance to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It might be worth while to remind him of these recommendations. It recommended that the governments of the three prairie provinces request an immediate investigation of the grocery retailing industry, under the Combines Investigation Act. Furthermore, the commission recommended that the three prairie provinces urge the federal Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to examine ways of eliminating the possibility of wasteful advertising and to prevent the use of advertising in the defence and fortification of positions of industry control. What has the minister done about this? How has he met this request?
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
As was to be expected the report of the commission stirred up some controversy. One of the grocery chains in western Canada published a vigorous denial of the charge that it had made any excessive profits in any area of Canada. But surely in this period of rampant price increases the consumers of this country deserve to know the truth from the minister who has the power to provide it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the New Democratic party I rise to support the motion of the official opposition which stands in the name of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). I believe the hon. member has made an excellent summary of the underlying conditions across this country and what the rising cost of living means to the many groups of people with moderate or low incomes. He referred to the fact that the former Minister of Transport had built an empire. If this is true I believe that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has gone him one better because he has founded a dynasty. Of course he did not do it alone. I wish to urge him to extend the congratulations of all of us in this group to his partner in this enterprise. I am glad he has had this achievement because I am going to score him now for some of the other things he has failed to do.
The cost of living is up again. The figures have been given by the hon. member who has just spoken. I remind hon. members that the figures for May this year show that the overall cost of living is up 4.7 per cent over May, 1968. The cost of food is up 4.2 per cent. Housing is up 5.3 per cent and transportation is up 5.2 p er cent These increases are a devastating indictment of the government's failure to deal with the cost of living and prevent it rising still higher.
Much has been said about the spectacular rise in the price of beef in recent weeks. Undoubtedly this is a matter of concern to

the consumer. Once again the boycotters are on the march with the minister in the role of cheerleader but, regrettably, from the sidelines. It would be a mistake to consider that all that is at stake is the price of beef. This is only one item in the whole broad spectrum of the rising cost of living which makes life a constant irritation for all Canadians and is a growing nightmare for those on low income. The people in comfortable middle-class circumstances find this irritating, but the people in the low income group find it a growing and terrible nightmare because they have no slack with which to cope with it.
The minister says that his job is to protect the consumer. He says that the trouble is that everyone wants to eat steaks and so the price must rise. He sees his role as one of advising the consumer to buy cheaper meat, perhaps hamburger. But what about the tens of thousands of Canadians who have never been able to afford steak and now see their hamburger costing close to $1 a pound? I remind the minister that these people cannot eat his advice any more than the people of Paris could eat the advice of Marie Antoinette when they could not get bread and she advised them to eat cake. I say that if the minister is to protect the consumer his job is to find out why the price of beef has risen so dramatically and why the whole cost of living has risen so dramatically and steadily. Who is responsible? Who is getting the profit?
Much has been made of the fact that we have two ministers whose opinions are at odds. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has been urging consumers to boycott beef and at the same time the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) has been greeting the substantial rise in the price of beef with loud hosannas.
I do not think anyone believes the farmer is responsible for the rise in the cost of beef or other meats. I do not believe it. I do not think that even the Minister of Agriculture believes it. I believe a great many people have failed to note page 2 of the statement of the Minister of Agriculture. On page 1 he says that he is delighted that beef prices are high and rising. But when you turn to page 2 you see these words:
Mr. Olson said he hopes most of the current price increase is passed on to farmers, because they are the ones who must make the basic adjustment if supply is to meet demand.
This has not always been the case. During the past to years, farmers have been receiving less and less of the dollar consumers spend on beef.
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
In 1949, they were receiving 68.5 cents of every dollar consumers spent on beef. In 1966, it was 54 cents.
I would like to know what it is now and so would the Canadian public. The Minister continues:
We don't have to search far to find out where the extra margin is going. Everyone involved in getting meat from the farm to the store shelf has had an increase. The farmer has not; yet it's the farmer who needs the money to produce the amount and quality of beef we want to buy in our stores.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
So there is no use making a scapegoat of the farmer or saying, "Poor farmer, he has waited so long for this increase and now he will get it". Even the Minister of Agriculture is just uttering a pious, forlorn hope that most of the increase will reach the farmer, because he knows that in the past such has not been the case. No one believes the farmer is responsible for increasing the price or that he will receive the benefit. Who, then, is responsible? I heard a broadcast the other day which indicated that speculators have found their way into this industry, too, that people with a few dollars to invest are buying cattle in the final stages of preparation for market- cattle in what the broadcaster termed "cattle boarding houses"-and are making a nice and speedy profit on the transaction. If this is going on the public has the right to know. If there is gambling in food futures the people have the right to know. Gambling in food futures must stop. The minister and the minister alone is responsible for ferreting out the facts. These are facts we must have.
I could go on to document various examples of rising prices. I have here in my desk a tin of sandwich paste, although I cannot display it because you have precluded such action, Mr. Speaker. Around the first of April it was selling at two tins for 27 cents. The price rose, and I can show this on the tin, to two tins for 39 cents as of May 27. Part way through this exercise a correspondent wrote his member of Parliament who duly communicated with the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The minister replied in part:
-considerable variation has occurred in the prices of the above product, due mainly to a price war among chain stores during the latter part of 1968 and the beginning of 1969.
He also stated that the company in question had provided specials during the last few
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers months of 1968 in order to meet competition. He then added:
It would appear that the two factors combined resulted in certain chain stores retailing Cordon Bleu meat paste at two for 27 cents for a period of time, after which the price returned to a selling level of two for 35 cents.
However, Mr. Speaker, the price did not stay there. On June 10 the same consumer said that since he had received the minister's answer the price had gone up from two for 39 cents on May 27 to two for 49 cents. I will let the minister have a look at this tin any time he wants to. This happened in two stores in the same town. The correspondent came to several conclusions. First of all he says there is no price war, minister or no minister, when you find the price going up and up steadily in more than one store. This means something else is at work. Second, he came to the conclusion that the profit on this sandwich paste must be in the neighbourhood of $1,000 per ton. When he remembered the big fuss and the investigation started by the late President Kennedy over the price increase of $6 per ton for steel, words failed him, and perhaps it is just as well.
He came to another conclusion, namely, that a very different attitude is taken in the matter of wage increases compared to price increases. He stated:
-as an employee our wages are greatly discussed before the annual working agreement is signed. It is then binding for one or two years, according to the marginal increase allowed.
This man is a trade unionist, and trade unions are not allowed to raise their wages at will. They have to go through a long period of discussion and red tape of various types during the collective bargaining process before any increase can be obtained.
What I want to know is this: If wages can be controlled in this way, why not prices? If wages can be held steady for one or two years after due deliberation and investigation, why not prices? These are the questions the public is asking the minister, but I regret to say that the minister is ducking them. The minister ducks for cover behind anything that it is possible to duck behind. The minister ducks behind the Economic Council. He says he cannot do anything until the Economic Council reports, but somehow this seems to be a receding horizon. He says he cannot do anything until the constitution is revamped because jurisdiction is divided with the provinces. The minister gives the impression that the provinces really have the lion's share of
10166	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16. 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers the responsibility in any event. So he ducks behind the constitution.
Is there anything to prevent the minister from sitting down, and discussing the problem with the provinces and then coming to an agreement? If there is, I have yet to hear it. The minister ducks behind his Prices and Incomes Commission. I do not know how long it is now we have waited to receive information as to who is to be appointed to the Prices and Incomes Commission. Somehow this too has become a receding horizon. We are getting information in little bits and pieces while the minister, as a means of avoiding action, ducks behind the fagade of the Prices and Incomes Commission which is not even set up yet.
I point out that all this new machinery in his department is costing a lot of money. The motion points out that it is going to cost nearly $16 million of the taxpayers' money to set up the machinery for this department to carry out its main purpose. I believe the taxpayers are entitled to see the minister take some kind of action. He may make mistakes, but who doesn't? One thing the taxpayers and the consumers of this country are not going to forgive is inactivity on the part of those who are unwilling to try certain things and simply sit and do nothing because they are afraid to do anything. All this machinery the minister is setting up could be used to good purpose. Somebody has said that the operation of it is exactly like a mill; if nothing is put into it it just grinds wind. I think nothing is being put in.
What are these groups investigating? What are they doing to justify the expenditure of this money? What are they doing to try to hold the price line or bring down the cost of living to the consumer? We have investigated housing, we have gone into transportation and dozens of other aspects of the cost of living which we believe are of concern; yet we have had not one scintilla of evidence that anything is being done about the cost of living. That is what the consumer cannot accept.
The minister evidently realizes how the Canadian public feels about this situation. I think he has a good deal of sympathy for the way they feel. After all, he is a consumer even though, like some of the rest of us, he is a well-padded one. At the Canadian Association of Consumers' annual meeting on June 11 he said:
Consumers "should" be fighting higher prices. Certainly, if "they" don't fight them, there is nobody else in the marketplace who is going to.
[Mrs. Maclnnis.l
I applaud that sentiment but I say that if consumers are going to fight against higher prices and the rising cost of living they deserve help and assistance from the minister. He is in the driver's seat where the controls are that should and could be exercised. Action is needed now in regard to meat prices. The situation in regard to beef prices ought to be another warning signal that the time has come for investigation and action.
Let me pinpoint the necessary steps. None of us wants to be regarded as being purely destructive in our criticism. People are suffering across the country and we want to see something done about it. We gain very little satisfaction in panning a government that is doing nothing. This government is obviously bankrupt of ideas or it does not have the courage to put its ideas into effect. You can take your choice. But we are going to attempt to see that our ideas are passed along to the people who sit in government. I am going to suggest several measures which are not new. They include several that we have urged over and over again. Perhaps they are new because they have never been used. In that sense they are brand new or store new, and they are worthy of a try.
First, there should be an immediate investigation into prices, beginning with beef prices. I am quite sure the farmers would say the same as the auto workers. I am sure they would say: "We do not mind you investigating the prices that we get for beef. Far from it, we want you to do so, but at the same time we expect that all the other people, including the speculators, the dealers, the people who own packing houses, the retailers and the wholesalers, will be investigated too." Wages, profits, prices, returns to the farmers and incomes of all sorts must be investigated in the package deal. Then people will be content to stand or fall by the result of such an investigation.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
There must be an investigation into prices.
I would rather it were conducted by a House of Commons committee so that the investigation would be carried out by a responsible body elected by the people of this country. If the minister insists on cluttering it up by making it a joint Senate-House of Commons committee, we will have to go along with that, but I see no reason why the investigation could not be carried out by a committee of the House of Commons responsible to this house. If other committees of the house are to
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
be sitting this summer in order to investigate matters, it is doubly important that one of them should be the consumers committee of the house.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
I would consider my summer well spent if I were able to sit on such a committee and investigate this matter. That is an emergency measure. The next step is a permanent prices review board which will not work in the dark of some office where the public cannot get at it. It should be a prices review board before which manufacturers and other agencies will have to appear and justify any price increases they want to make. Let there be light on this subject. It is all this secrecy which creates public mistrust. Let these matters be brought fully before the public.
Rather than introducing half-baked amendments to the Combines Investigation Act that would allow its present restrictive jurisdiction to be interpreted a little more freely, we should bring in measures to afford real protection to the Consumer. The minister should either throw out the Combines Investigation Act altogether and bring in a piece of legislation with teeth in it, or provide the poor old Combines Investigation Act with real teeth that can be used on monopolies, cartels and all the other agencies that are applying a stranglehold to the neck of the consumer.
I say in closing, Mr. Speaker, that we in this corner of the house have sympathy for the minister. We think he has one of the toughest jobs there is. We do not think he yet knows the half of it, because if the cost of living is allowed to creep up and up and pensions and low incomes are allowed to stay where they are, if the gap between income and the cost of living widens, the minister will find he has a great deal more trouble to cope in the future.
Let the minister seek his real allies. His only real allies are the consumers of the country. Let him carry out his work in such a way that the people of this country know what he is doing. Let him turn the searchlight of publicity on what he and the department are trying to do to solve this problem. When the prices committee was set up two years ago the minister said that what triggered it off was the fact that the boycotters had the courage to march and raise a fuss about prices. I tell the minister that the boycotters are again on the prowl. If the minister is wise
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers he will again establish a consumers committee of the house to investigate fully the increasing cost of living. He will proceed from there to have not just study groups, seminars and high level, ivory tower enterprises involved in this question, but he will really get to work, put his back into it and take those steps that are necessary to bring down the cost of living.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the opposition is quite relevant to the situation which prevails at this time in Canada. It reads as follows:
That this house condemns the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs for his failure to protect Canadian consumers from the crippling burden of ever-increasing prices and, in particular, from the recent exorbitant jump in food and rent costs, despite this house's allocation of nearly $16 million to his department for the main purpose of averting such developments.
Mr. Speaker, since the end of the war, that is since 1945, prices have climbed steadily. At that time we had a government led by the Right Hon. Mackenzie King and prices were going up. The Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent succeeded Mackenzie King and prices kept on rising.
In 1957, when a Progressive Conservative government came to power, prices kept going up as usual.
A Liberal government succeeded a Progressive Conservative government in 1963, and prices were still going up.
In 1968, we turned to a government promoting the establishment of a just society and we are still looking for that just society because prices are sky rocketing.
However, this is paradoxical because the Conservatives, who introduce such a motion, fail as usual to suggest a solution.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis), a representative of the New Democratic party, has just made a first rate speech but, as far as a concrete solution is concerned, should we only provide for the establishment of a parliamentary committee to study prices, to inquire in the West, in the East and in the central provinces of Canada in order to see whether it is true that prices are high, that some company is making profits, or that salaries have gone up?
Mr. Speaker, that is not a solution. It is not by creating new committees and by dreaming up new government devices that we shall succeed in keeping prices at a reasonable level.
10168	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16. 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
There are solutions and I will give some in a tew minutes.
But at the present time, Mr. Speaker, we must bow to the fact that since the appointment of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs-that department exists only since the beginning of the present parliament-prices have spiralled.
Why was a Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs appointed? To conceal the perfidy of a system that crushes and cheats everybody. And while the minister is traveling across Canada, exploiters keep on exploiting people and neither the producers nor the consumers are benefiting but the intermediate bodies that are precisely protected by this government wile, which supports some people protected by the government who manipulate prices.
There is also the deplorable fact of the many strikes Canada cannot afford and which do increase the cost of goods, such as bulding materials. Every now and again there is a strike that leads to higher prices. Union leaders have yet to understand that.
This is so true that when a union-and please note that I am in favour of unions provided their members are respected- obtains a salary increase of 50c. or 75c. an hour for its members, that increase is reflected in a price increase of 75c., 85c. or even $1.00 an hour.
Finally, the consumer always pays, but the union leaders are not always honest enough to explain the situation to their members. That is why we witness the present spectacle that creates misery in the face of abundance.
Mr. Speaker, salary increases are not the only ones that are reflected in higher prices. There is also the drive for bigger profits. But one evil does not cure the other. Both are responsible. Demands must be reasonable. However, the worker must not be blamed for requesting a more decent standard of living.
The situation must be seen as it is and, as I said a while ago, when a 30c. or 50c. an hour increase is granted a worker, prices go up accordingly.
Thus the worker is always losing ground because of the increase in consumer prices.
Mr. Speaker, I said a while ago that the middlemen, the speculators get rich while the producer does not. His situation is even more deplorable. The western wheat growers, the eastern milk producers, the butter producers,

the corn producers in Ontario, the producers of textile products in the Eastern Townships, the wood producers in my area or in the areas of British Columbia, in short, those who are really producers are literally robbed just as the consumer is.
On the one hand,, the producer is in a bad spot; on the other hand, the consumer has not got the purchasing power to acquire goods or to buy what he needs. And the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford) wants to investigate. An investigation on prices. This is not so difficult since we all know that prices are very high. In every field we know that there is a constant increase.
Recently the price of meat, for instance, skyrocketed. This compels the people, especially the poor, to eat baloney or hot dogs, which does not always help to keep the family or the children in good health.
One has to buy cheaper meat instead of the best grade meat which costs too much, molasses instead of maple syrup, and so on.
In any event, Mr. Speaker, with his income, the consumer cannot afford to face the cost of living. What do we, Creditistes, suggest to the government and the minister? That a new inquiry commission be established? That $16 million be spent to find out whether it is true that prices are high?
We know prices are high. So, the minister and the government must take action. To help the consumer, we ask for a compensated retail discount, a discount to the consumer for which the retailer is compensated. That would cost much less than the money spent on inquiries. Thus, the consumer's purchasing power would be increased while protecting the producer and the retailer.
It seems to me that it should be worth a try. But no! Because it is a Social Credit idea, they think it is funny. But, no one else has any solution to offer. Neither the opposition, nor the New Democratic party, nor the government, nobody has any solution. They want to institute inquiries.
People say: this one or that one made a fortune at the expense of the producer and the retailer. There are such cases. But there exist in Canada some laws to take care of cartels, of unscrupulous people, of those who work against the common good. And when a man or a company are caught red-handed, if instead of being fined $25,000, they had to spend 10 years in jail, the results would be different because those people would not want to be imprisoned.
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
A $25,000 fine is not too painful because the manufacturer immediately increases his prices by 1 or 2 per cent and makes a profit of 50 or 75 million, which helps him pay the fine. Imprisonment is another matter.
This act, that is the Combines Investigation Act, should be applicable to those who work against the common good. But it is not. Why? Because the government is afraid.
For window-dressing, a Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is appointed. This will relieve the consumer and convince him that he can continue to live without eating. This will convince the producer that he has merely to produce and draw a small income. This will convince everybody that the government does not want to act, but the entire population are being put off with fine words by the government and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservatives' motion deals with the constant rise in prices, especially the unrestrained increase in food and rent costs.
As for rents, what is being done? Is a laborer who earns $4,000 per year in a position to pay a monthly rent of $175? Poor families are compelled to live in slums and shacks. We see such shacks throughout Canada, a country which is said to be the richest in the world in natural resources.
If you visit the suburbs of Montreal, Quebec, Trois-Rivieres, Toronto and Winnipeg, you will see that the problem is not a matter of language, French or English, but of slums throughout the country. When people die of starvation, no matter if they speak English or French, they do not feed themselves with their language. Poor people will eat only if they get food.
That point has not been grasped yet and people are left to their divisions and quarrels. There is talk of decent dwellings and of new legislation on housing. If one wants to build a house today-and the minister is well aware of the fact-the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation or the insurance companies charge interest rates of 10 or 12 per cent. Under the current interest rate, a $20,000 house payable over a 40-year period will cost $99,900.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
I do not believe a word of it when the government says that it wants to fight inflation. Why does the government not allow loans for housing at a maximum interest rate of 3 per cent, that is the administrative costs,
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers instead of loans at 10 or 12 per cent? They say they want to promote the construction of houses, so that payments can be lower. But as interest charges increase monthly instalments, repayment terms are extended from 30 to 40 years. The term is extended so that the consumer will pay more.
Mr. Speaker, not a single Canadian worker can afford the luxury-and it should not be a luxury

of owning his own house today. Even contractors have to borrow money at 9 and 10 per cent because of that system, and there is nothing the government can do.
Once again, the opposition has nothing to propose. They say the government does not behave well. What would they do in its place? Absolutely nothing. They do not know and they offer no solutions.
As for me, I have a solution to propose: housing for Canadian citizens at an interest rate not above 3 per cent.
And here is something even better than that: to truly help Canadians to become home owners, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation should get the credit it needs from the Bank of Canada, without interest, as it is done for foreign countries.
I do believe we must help foreign countries, but it is time we started helping the Canadians who build Canada to house themselves properly, to eat properly, to dress properly. For that, there is need of a definite policy, a policy which will make it possible to tackie the problem that holds everything up, that is, the financing problem: there is the rub!
But the government says the same thing over and over again: let us impose new taxes; let us increase taxes.
So we suggest that something must be done to put some order in our finance, in the money of Canada, in the Canadian monetary system and that it is time to stop crushing the producer as well as the consumer in Canada. Thus let us begin by putting some order in the monetary system. Money should truly reflect the wealth of Canada. We must not print money irresponsibly, as the minister already said, with a machine to make money. Money must not be printed in an irresponsible and unrestricted way.
However, we must take into account that it is possible for the Canadian people to make some real achievement in Canada. The government must assume its responsibilities, in connection with the monetary system, and we shall then be in a position to fight effectively
10170	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers and efficiently the rising cost of living and this shameful exploitation of the Canadian people.
When we speak of the consumer, we mean everybody, not only the miner working for Noranda Mining, in my area, but also the farmer in Beaudry, the people in Val d'Or, the leader of the N.D.P. (Mr. Douglas) and myself. However, Mr. Speaker, we must realize that a pound of butter costs just as much to the follow making $2,000 a year as to the member of parliament who is getting $18,000 a year. Clothing costs the same also and low-income people cannot even think of buying all they need. Why? Because they lack buying power. I suggest two solutions to this problem:	either increase the buying power
through a divident guaranteed by Canada's productivity, or through a compensated discount on consumer prices, which would benefit the consumer and would be compensated to the retailer who provides the goods and the services.
Mr. Speaker, those are two solutions we recommend. And the minister should consider them because he knows that with the present system he is just running around like a dog trying to bite its tail and never catching it.
So, Mr. Speaker, changes are due, and it is the responsibility of the government and the minister. Our responsibility is to suggest concrete steps to the minister, as I just did.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in
entering this debate may I first thank the mover of the motion and the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) for their kind good wishes to me and my wife on the occasion of an addition to the family over the weekend. I understand there has been some concern in the house; I should like to assure hon. members that he has hair somewhat longer than his father's.
Before going further I should like to congratulate the opposition on what is obviously a new-found interest in the price of beef. One might consider, looking at this motion and listening to the speeches so far, that the question of beef prices and meat prices generally has been one of abiding interest to many members of the opposition for weeks and weeks. Nevertheless, I looked carefully through the record of the budget debate which took place only last week and found that not once was the question of beef prices raised on that occasion.

DEBATES	June 16, 1969
Again, the estimates of the department must be of some concern, because the motion talks about an allocation of some $16 million to my ministry. Well, my estimates were before the committee a week ago last Thursday, and members of the opposition thought I was doing such a fine job as minister-the program was so good-that they were passed in three hours during which time not once was a question asked about beef prices or about rent costs or about the Prices and Incomes Commission.
Some concern is shown in this motion about rents, which are exceedingly high. I shall not deal with the subject of housing because that is the responsibility of one of my colleagues. I do suggest, however, that more would be done to reduce rents if the house would give third reading as quickly as possible to Bill C-195, reflecting the government's housing program, rather than involving this chamber in the demagogic debate it has heard so far from the opposition this afternoon.
I realize that the hon. member who moved this motion is new to the house, though the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway is not. I find it startling that there should be errors in the motion itself. The motion states that the house has allocated $16 million to the department for the main purpose of averting certain unfavourable price developments. I am sorry the opposition is so little concerned about the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs as to pay no attention to what is said when estimates are before the committee. It was explained to the committee that some 68 per cent of the budget of the department is offset by its revenues; it is not a complete drain on general revenue as the motion implies. Out of the total budget of the department, some $6.5 million is voted to the corporate affairs bureau, to the operation of the patent office, the trade marks office, the corporations branch and the bankruptcy branch. I would have thought the opposition, bearing in mind its abiding interest in this matter, would at least have secured enough information about the department to have got the figures right.
Nevertheless, I do feel complimented by the fact that the opposition has singled out my department as the one to which its motions should be directed, and has tried to place blame upon me for the high prices of beef, meat generally, food and rents. It seems to me, though, that this is a motion which could just as well have been directed to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. June 16, 1969	COMMONS
Pepin) or to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson). I can only conclude it was directed to me because members of the opposition felt the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was doing such a good job that they should move a motion to try to destroy some of the popularity it has with the people.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Everyone, including the government, is concerned about the rate at which prices and costs have been increasing in Canada. We are concerned about this both as consumers and as producers in the economy. There is no question that our prices and costs performance in Canada has been unsatisfactory for some time. The consumer price index has been rising in our view, as well as in the view of the opposition, at quite unacceptable rates-rates in excess of 4 per cent per annum.
The burden on the consumer is obvious, but the problem lies much deeper and I think it is good to reiterate this time and time again. As an international trading country our prosperity and prospects for development depend on our ability to sell abroad. Our exports have been running at record levels and we must continue to export at those levels. This means that, as a government and as a country, we have to keep our costs and prices in line with those of other countries. Indeed, we must try to do a little better than other countries and, generally speaking, we have been succeeding.
It is important to look at the situation in which many of our farmers find themselves, having to sell their products in a highly competitive world market when they are able to sell them at all. Yet at the same time the farmers are caught in a vicious cost-price squeeze through which almost everything they buy-their land, their tractors and implements, their fencing and binder twine-is at inflationary prices.
Looking at the question from another angle, let us consider the effects of inflation on personal savings. If our growth and development are to continue we must maintain a very high level of personal savings in Canada, and we cannot allow these savings to be devalued by inflation.
As hon. members have pointed out, this is far more than an economic problem, and we must recognize the importance of it as such. The government and I are also highly sensitive to the human aspect of inflation. Here I am talking about the people the hon. member
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers who moved the motion talked about, those who suffer first and who suffer the most. They are the economically weak, the unorganized, the elderly, the disabled pensioners and the poor. They cannot protect themselves, whereas the well organized and the economically strong can. They have the economic power to keep up with the trend in prices by bargaining for higher wages, by fixing higher professional fees if they are members of a profession, by raising rents if they are the owners of real property. Some businessmen are in a position to pass cost increases along to their customers in the form of higher prices. Unions can strive for a better deal at the bargaining table.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
All these things give relief to those with market power, but they only aggravate the problem for others and ultimately for everybody, themselves included. Meanwhile the first and the hardest hit are those Canadians who cannot protect themselves from the effect of higher prices. They are not organized to insist that their incomes match rising costs. They have no power to insist on a fair share.
I have said before and say again that a fixed income must not mean a fixed injustice. People without bargaining power cannot bargain for a better deal. It is no exaggeration to say that every man who irresponsibly raises costs is personally inflicting an injustice on a poor family, on a blind pensioner, or on an elderly retired couple.
This resolution focuses upon the cost of living, a matter of obvious concern to every member of the public. At the outset, however, I would be remiss if I did not state with some force that Canadians, along with citizens of perhaps one or two other countries, enjoy the highest standard of living in the world. This is a fact. It does not, however, deter us from seeking, by all means available to us, to maintain and improve that standard of living for all our citizens in every region of the country.
The cost of living has been going up at an unacceptable rate. The cost of goods to the consumer reflects, in part at least, rising costs incurred by producers and manufacturers. All these costs are, in large part, a reflection of the general upward trend of prices. The stabilizing or improvement of the cost of living, therefore, is to be accomplished by containing the forces of inflation.
Many factors affect the general rate of increase or decrease of the price level. I am,
29180-643J
10172	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers however, aware that we do not know as much as we need to know about the forces that foster and accelerate inflation. There are those who question that statement, but I think the three speeches to which we have just listened, which contained very few ideas and new proposals in regard to what we should be doing, demonstrate that we need to know more about the problem of inflation and how to alleviate it. It is to increase our knowledge in this field that I am setting up the Prices and Incomes Commission which will study this problem as one of its specific tasks.
I can say, however, that no one department can by itself fully control these forces and no single policy will bring about a solution. It is a complicated problem requiring a combination of sophisticated measures. The government has available to it a range of policy instruments developed over the years, and it is using those instruments. The most important and continuing tool available to meet inflation is, and will continue to be, monetary and fiscal policy.
I think other factors also ought to be mentioned. On the demand side, the rate of growth in federal government spending on goods and services has been sharply reduced and efforts continue to be made to restrain other forms of federal expenditure. Part of the problem is that every time we try to reduce government expenditure by cutting out or by proposing to cut out a program, all hell breaks loose in the opposition and objection is taken to such proposals. Hon. members opposite speak glibly of the need to reduce expenditure, but every time we try to do so we receive nothing but complaints from hon. members opposite.

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Industrial development programs and research incentives designed to raise productivity are being implemented by the government. In its procurement policies the government of Canada has reorganized and centralized its operations to bring to bear the fullest measure of competition for supply contracts.
Canada's trade policy is being aimed at progressively extending the benefits of efficiency and cost reduction to be realized from international specialization. We are also impressed with the growing importance of wage and salary bargaining in the public sector as a factor in the movement of costs and prices, and we have been exercising for the last year a restraining influence in that area.
It is of particular importance, in my view, to develop the efficient operation of the price mechanism in our economy which in very large part depends upon very well informed consumers and upon the power of consumers to make their preferences felt in the marketplace. This is one of the fundamental objectives of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The exercise of market power by informed consumers should have a moderating influence on the movement of prices.
Inflation is a world-wide phenomenon, but let there be no misunderstanding about it: my
June IB, 1969	COMMONS
colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) has, I think, made clear that the government is determined to end this intolerable rate of inflation and control the inflationary pressures in our economy. But unlike what the opposition suggests, this cannot be done by wishing. It cannot be done through simplistic solutions. It requires action on a number of fronts.
As I have explained, the most important of these is fiscal policy. In his recent budget my colleague the Minister of Finance forecast a surplus of $250 million. Lest anyone misunderstand the importance of that surplus let me point out, as he did, that it represents a change from the budget deficit of $566 million in 1968-69, meaning a swing in the economic impact of the budget of almost $1 billion, considerably more than one per cent of Canada's gross national product. I regret that the opposition, which is so concerned about inflation, is putting forward every day in this house some proposal to spend the budget surplus and thus put the government back into a deficit position. These financial measures, combined with monetary policy, are designed to provide a check on inflationary forces, and will ease the strain in capital markets. To keep the brakes on, the government is continuing the existing surtax on personal income tax and corporation income tax for 1968 and 1969 by extending it until December 31, 1970. The deferral of capital cost allowances in overheated areas of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia is a selective measure to cool down the situation without strangling necessary building.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
The budget address also announced tariff reductions to step up the last three stages of Canada's implementation of the Kennedy Round so that they will take effect immediately. This meant an immediate reduction of tariffs averaging about three percentage points on imports valued at $2 billion annually. In adopting these selective tariff cuts immediately, it was the government's view that increased competition would result which would in turn put downward pressure on prices. I was glad to see that some of the opposition members who spoke in the budget debate agreed that would be the case.
Cost savings to manufacturers and distributors should be achieved through the tariff cuts themselves at the same time that imports or the threat of imports places pressure on the domestic market. All this should help
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers keep down prices and benefit the consumer. It is, of course, difficult to forecast with any precision when and how the effects of the tariff reductions will be felt. Indeed, they may be positive effects which can be obscured by unrelated cost increasing factors such as transportation costs, crop shortages, wage increases, and so on.
We hope, however, to do everything within our power to ensure that increased competition are left free to bring about the necessary adjustments. My officials will make every effort to ensure that increased competition is not negated through price fixing or any other form of illegal conspiracy or restrictive practice.
The level of government expenditures is very important and I am sure some of you, if one can judge by opposition speeches, think absolutely nothing has been done in this regard. But the budget surplus did not just happen. The government recognizes the overriding need to keep its fiscal house in order. The opposition seem to forget such things as the end of the winter works program, the decision against proceeding with the Prince Edward Island causeway, the abandonment of the Queen Elizabeth telescope in my own province, the freeze on the public service. The opposition said we needed a surplus, yet opposed cancelling these projects. Over the last year all government programs came under scruting, with reduced expenditures in some cases and in other cases decisions against beginning desirable programs.
It is clear that the government has a major role to play in ending inflation and is determined to do its part. But it is too easy to say, as many do, that this is just a matter for the government. Attitudes in the private sector have to change if we are to bring inflation under control in an orderly way. There is no reason to doubt that governments can stop inflation. But some ways of bringing inflation to a halt are more painful than others. This is where the attitudes of private business, trade unions and individuals will be crucial.
The more restraint people in all walks of life are prepared to exercise in their pursuit of higher incomes the less need there will be for the government to slow down our rate of economic growth. People will have to adjust their sights to the prospect of price stability. What does this mean? It means that businesses should no longer assume that they can increase their prices without danger of losing their market. They should no longer assume that the extra cost of whatever wage
10174	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers increases they accede to can readily be passed on to the public. They should no longer assume that whatever new investments they may choose to make will pay off through an inflationary rise in demand for their products. It means that errors and excesses can no longer be expected to be painted over by inflation. The chickens will come home to roost. It means that trade unions generally will have to adjust their sights to annual rates of wage increases that are consistent with the rate of growth of productivity in our economy.
The decision, announced in the budget, to accelerate the rate of tariff reduction, indeed to put the whole of the Kennedy Round tariff reductions in force in one step, is designed to introduce more price competition into the Canadian economy at the time when we need it most. This should make a significant contribution to slowing down inflationary trends. Those businesses that are protected by the tariff against external competition are often the leaders in inflationary price increases.
I have talked about the role of government. There is a responsibility on everyone, on all hon. members and the consumers they represent. The individual consumer can make a contribution both to his own welfare and that of others. He must take advantage of a competitive situation, where it truly is competitive. That is to say, he should resist high prices and refuse to buy shoddy merchandise. The committee that Senator Croll and I chaired on consumer prices, of which the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway was a member, made the point that consumers can affect the prices of items simply by not buying them if they think the price is excessive, that in many cases there are substitutes or alternatives. This was said in relation to food but is equally true and more pertinent when talking about clothing, credit and loans, furnishings, automobiles; appliances, almost everything the consumer buys. So I urge consumers to inform themselves of the various prices offered, to shop around. If consumers are careless about their purchasing they are going to pay more.
Many consumers are disturbed about the price of beef, which has increased sharply in the last few weeks. I have already made some public statements on this question, but I want to explain briefly how this situation developed.
At the outset, I should emphasize that cattle prices are determined on the North American market and not in Canada alone. IMr. BasfordJ
DEBATES	June 16, 1969
We have in this country roughly 10 per cent of the combined Canada-United States cattle supply. Obviously, whether we are exporting or importing cattle, there is going to be a well-defined relationship between prices in Canada and in the major U.S. cattle markets. Choice steers were selling in the United States in February at about $29.50 a hundredweight-that is live weight, Mr. Speaker-but within recent weeks the price has advanced to around $35 a hundred, U.S. dollars. Canadian prices inevitably followed this trend.
One of the reasons for the increase in prices is that cattle numbers in North America have not been increasing fast enough to keep up with the population growth and with the desire of Canadians and the people of the United States to eat more beef. In 1960 the people of the United States ate 99 pounds per capita; in 1968 this rose to 109 pounds and for this year the estimate is 111 pounds. In Canada the estimated per capita consumption of beef in 1960 was 70 pounds, but it has risen now to about 90 pounds. This is partly a reflection of rising income levels during that period. Beef eating, in other words, increases with affluence. There is a seasonal aspect to the recent price increases in addition.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
The market naturally adjusts to the changing supply and demand situation. In Toronto in January supermarkets were paying 51 cents to 52 cents a pound for red brand beef sides. By early June the price had increased to 63 cents to 65 cents a pound. Some of the choice cuts make up a relatively small proportion of the total carcass and their scarcity is reflected in the sharp increases for such things as porterhouse and sirloin steaks.
When a situation like this develops some people start looking around for somebody to blame and, depending on their point of view, they will pick on the farmers, the meat packers or the supermarkets. We are facing the consequences of living in a market economy and there is no question that the market will remedy the present shortage even though this will take some time. In the meantime, I have said to Canadian consumers that they should diversify their diet a little more and search around for some substitute for cuts of beef which they think are too high in price. If North American housewives would be more discriminating in their purchases of meat the demand pressure would let up a little. This is a powerful weapon in the hands of consumers and I hope they will use it.
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
I trust that it will be evident to all from what I have said that any direct intervention by the federal government to control beef prices is not a practical solution. Only a few months ago we had demands from some of the parties in this house that we intervene in the lumber market, and even that we nationalize the lumber industry because of the record prices and market situation. The position in that industry has now been completely reversed. Prices are away down from what they were three months ago, and in some places mills are closing.
I have been reviewing over-all government policy developments. I should now like to outline the specific role of my department in resisting the upward trend of prices.
