speechtext:
I am grateful to the opposition for allowing me to continue. In conclusion I want to discuss the specific role of my department in resisting the upward trend of prices.
It is important that there be a clear understanding of the role of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. In simple terms it is the department's function to promote the efficient operation of our competitive market economy. I have repeatedly stated in the house that we are dependent for the level of prices of particular goods, as well as the general price level, upon the operation of market forces. Perhaps, therefore, I should state quite briefly what the concept of a competitive market economy means.
In the light of the confusion in the mind of the hon. member who moved the motion I must take this occasion once again to make it clear that this department was not established as an instrument of price control. This was made very clear in the debates at that time, and I hope the hon. member will reread them. The primary purpose of our consumer affairs program is to protect the consumer in the market, to improve his capacity for making choices, and generally to make the market work more effectively. To the extent that we succeed in improving the way the market works we should have some moderating influence on prices, but the general price level
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers will continue to be affected by broad economic forces. These forces are, of course, the concern of the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada.
I should like to point out that in the short period of 18 months since my department came into existence we have initiated a program of sizeable proportions directed toward the improvement of both the demand and supply sides of the marketplace. I should like to describe this program in terms of two main functions, competition and information.
Several major departments can have an influence on the competitive policy of Canada. However, it falls to my department to be the focal point of competition policy. The Combines Investigation Act constitutes the embodiment of parliament's decision, made as long ago as 1889, to maintain a competitive market economy in Canada by prohibiting collusive and monopolistic restraints on the competitive process by the business community. This act seeks to keep the market free in those areas not otherwise regulated by valid provincial or federal laws.
The market should therefore be kept free to provide for consumers the best choice that can be made available of product, quality and price. Only if these choices are available can the consumer effectively exercise his sovereignty. Only if the market is freely accessible to newcomers will pressure be placed upon older established industries to seek ways to reduce their costs and improve their efficiency and pass on the result of such savings to the ultimate consumer.
One of the mechanisms provided in the act is the ability to reduce or eliminate the tariff on goods that are found by an inquiry to be subjected to restrictive practices, and this is a remedy which I am already seeking to develop. However, this legislation requires much improvement to make it fully effective. The director and his staff require a very significant increase in their resources merely to carry out the work that they have in hand. They, of course, have had to take their share of the government's determined program to reduce the costs of the public service.
Important areas of the Combines Investigation Act are in need of revision to make them more effective for current tasks. This is particularly true in the case of the provisions relating to mergers and monopolies. There is also a gap in the legislation to the extent that it does not cover many services which now make an important contribution to the gross
10176	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers national product. As hon. members are aware, this whole question is now under study by the Economic Council of Canada which is expected to report this month. When I have received the report, and I give the house this undertaking, I intend to move with all speed toward a revision of these laws. I have already taken preliminary steps within my department to receive the report and commence revising the Combines Investigation Act.
1 know that there are some members of the house who feel that we should have a new act right away. I think it would be very difficult to revise the act without first having a report from the Economic Council, and I think parliament would be foolish to consider such a revision until it had that report. The deputy leader of the N.D.P. appeared to agree with that position the other day.
I would like to mention one particular program of my department because I think it shows up the hypocrisy of the opposition this afternoon. As a further contribution to the more efficient operation of the market the government introduced Bill C-102 to weaken, in the case of prescription drugs, the patent and trade mark protection that has contributed in such an important degree to the lack of price competition in this market, and which contributed to the very high cost of prescription drugs. This afternoon we heard great eloquence from the opposition on behalf of the poor people, the people who cannot afford things that are priced so highly. But look at their record on Bill C-102. They opposed it both in this house and in the Senate. Had it not been for the members of the Official Opposition that legislation probably would have been in effect a year ago during which time it could have worked to reduce the cost of prescription drugs. So, Mr. Speaker, I was touched but rather cynical about the opposition's expressions of concern for the poor, remembering their record on Bill C-102.

Six months ago I issued a white paper on policies for price stability in which I reviewed the current trend of prices, and emphasized the need to develop new techniques to supplement fiscal and monetary policy which are the most important means of dealing with such situations. Much has been said this afternoon about this and much has been said by the representative of the New Democratic party concerning the need for a [Mr. Basford.l
DEBATES	June 16, 1969
prices and incomes review board. I should like to discuss the Batten report. The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway had much to say about the need for a prices and incomes review board, and she has always chided me for not implementing the Batten report. I should like simply to quote the Batten report which seems to be her bible. It states:
This commission recommends against the creation of prices review boards, price control boards, or guideline policies. These are much more apt to conceal the real problems underlying and causing inflation and to confuse the issues, than they are to achieve any substantial successes.
So I should like the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway to reread the Batten report and reread what it suggests should be done. This is the reason we have not had a prices review board. This is why we have stated in the white paper the intention of establishing a Prices and Incomes Commission to examine the various causes of inflation and suggest to the government and the private sector possible courses of action to follow.
Although the inflationary trend is world wide we believe that this measure, the establishing of this commission, will make some contribution toward containing inflation in this country. My view is shared by Dr. Young, the chairman, a prominent and highly respected Canadian economist whose appointment I think has been welcomed by people across the country. In connection with the work of the commission, Dr. Young has said there are good grounds for believing the stated aims of the Canadian and United States governments that they intend to control inflation, and that there are good grounds for thinking that those who are betting on the continuation of a high rate or price increases will be proved wrong.
The Commission will be asked to inquire into and report upon the causes, processes and consequences of inflation and to inform those making current prices and income decisions, the general public and the government, on how price stability may best be achieved. They will undertake continued studies and investigations to this end and will publish reports. I am confident that the commission, as it proceeds with this task of giving public advice on how we may achieve better price stability, will be able to bring about a greater degree of restraint on the part of those in the private sector who are charged with the responsibility of making current decisions about prices and incomes. This will provide information that will assist those who determine
June 1G, 1969	COMMONS
policies with respect to prices and wages to make their decisions in such a way as to reduce the upward pressure on prices. The Commission can make a valuable contribution toward price stability only if it gets the cooperation it will need from all parties concerned.
I should add that prices and incomes policies having similar objectives have been instituted in other countries. We have been at pains to examine their experiences and to avoid the defects that have been apparent in them. For one thing, we are making it clear that the role of the commission is not a substitute for monetary and fiscal policy and other inflationary policies, but it is a supplementary policy supporting them.
Another aspect in which our policy differs from other countries is that we intend to establish a joint parliamentary committee to receive and to study the reports of the commission. I thought the order to establish the committee would be on the order paper today. Apparently it will be on the order paper tomorrow. This will be in accordance with the intention stated in the white paper. This will enable public debate to develop with respect to the information and recommendations made by the commission.
The joint committee will have a very important function to perform in calling witnesses, consulting experts and debating generally the ways and means which the Commission suggests for minimizing inflationary tendencies. This process of debate will further serve to heighten the awareness of business and labour groups, provincial and municipal governments and consumers at large of the situations that are causing the upward pressure on prices and ways in which they may be counteracted.
Therefore in outlining both the policies of the government generally with regard to inflation and the role of my department specifically, I think we have disclosed a consciousness of the concern expressed today by the opposition and the concern expressed in the motion before the house. I think the record of the government is one which indicates that we certainly do not have to take a back seat to the opposition in our concern for those problems and the effectiveness of our policies in dealing with them.

First of all, there 'was a lecture which we have heard before concerning our sympathy for the pensioners, the veterans, the poor people and others on fixed, low incomes. With that I have no argument. Then he gave us a few suggestions about which I will have something to say. After that there was a package of abuse in which he tried to say that all the responsibility for the lack of action was due to the attitude of the opposition. Then there were a few promises for the future.
I should like to come to grips immediately with the first point. I could not help but agree with him. He had the whole house in the palm of his hand when he talked about the pensioners, the poor, the veterans and those on fixed incomes. We are really aware of what he said when he talked about these people. He asked who is to blame if he has failed in his responsibility in this new department. He said he would tell us who is to blame. He said it is all the Canadian housewives because they do not know how to shop and do not know how to buy. That is who is to blame. His second solution is to boycott. Then he said that the opposition has nothing to offer. So I shall start off by quoting a question I put the other day to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Let us find out what his answer was because at that time every Member of Parliament could have asked the same question. My question, as recorded on page 10036 of Hansard, was:
I should like to ask the minister whether he has given some thought to having the combines investigation branch look into the chain stores to

find out whether there is a monopoly on beef because of the wide spread between what the producer is getting and what the consumer is paying for it.
If I might digress for a moment I should like to say I made it my business today to call the city of Calgary to find out what beef is worth on the hoof, What it is worth wholesale and what it is worth retail. [DOT] (4:40 p.m.)

Then the leader of the N.D.P. put a very powerful supplementary question. He asked, and I paraphrase, whether, in view of the fact there is a good deal of evidence that some exploitation is going on in the rapid increase in the price of beef, referring to the difference between what the producer is getting and what the consumer is paying, the minister would take the matter in hand and get the director to act. I wish he would send it along to me.

I believe that the minister, with the department he has and the law officers he has at his fingertips, should initiate an investigation by the director.
Instead, the minister today has indicted the ranchers. I am going to refer to that in a few minutes. He has got into a quarrel with another minister because they are on opposite sides of the situation at the same time. He has also indicted every housewife who goes shopping. He said they do not know what they are

doing and this is causing the trouble. Let us take a look at the situation.
At the stockyards in Calgary beef from one of the great beef producing areas of Canada is selling for 32 cents or 33 cents a pound. I will give the prices for the various cuts. T-bone, club and porterhouse steaks are selling for $1.89 per pound. Last year steak was selling for about $1.19 per pound. I am .well aware of the cost of getting this meat off the hoof and onto the plates of consumers. Let us take a look at what happens to beef. A yearling steer is taken to market- most of our beef comes from this source-and is sold in the stockyard at 32 cents to 33 cents per pound. It will weight about 800 to 900 pounds, more or less, and will dress out at approximately 60 per cent of live weight or 480 to 500 pounds. How, then, does the minister explain the price moving up by 68 cents a pound in the stores and only three cents, four cents or five cents a pound on the hoof? I have almost finished, Mr. Speaker. We in the opposition have warned the government about the inflationary trends. We continually pointed this out when they advanced grandiose programs and talked
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers about cutting expenditures, at the same time continuing to outspend all other levels of government. I tell the house frankly that recently I missed a vote in the house. I have not missed very many. That vote was on the languages bill. If I had been here I would have voted to send the bill to committee.
I received the other day some information from a government department. I shall not say which department it was. The information I received was not in the area we are discussing at the moment. This is just one example of waste and inadequate planning by the government. The government set aside $125,000 to change a traffic circle on the trans-Canada highway at Banff. That program has been cancelled or delayed. What will they do with the $125,000? They put up new signs in Banff last year, and they will take that money and spend it on further new signs. This is a government that is supposed to be cutting costs. I am sure that all those people who believe we have a great nation made up of two great cultures and languages are of the opinion that at this stage, in a place like Banff, this is one expense we could avoid for another year. This is just one example of the wasteful expenditure of the government.
I object very strongly to the minister saying that the opposition is asking for programs to be implemented that will cause greater expenditures. I ask him to show me anywhere in Hansard where I have stood in my place and asked that more money be spent. I would like to see some of our taxes cut. The main plank of the government's budget was to impose a surtax in order to stop inflation. That surtax is against the people with fixed incomes and against the people living on pensions. It is making them poorer and poorer and it is making it more difficult for them to fight an inflation which the government created.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
Members on the government side are trying to ride two horses at once. I was impressed with the speech of the Leader of the Rallie-ment Creditiste when he spoke this afternoon. He did not ride two horses at once-he pointed to the problem. Government members try to have a great love affair with producers and with labour. They are only encouraging the ever-spiralling inflationary trend which drives wages up to buy consumer goods. Profits go up to pay the wages. So the bitter struggle goes on until the government finds a solution to the problem. The government might have to go back to the 30 per cent
10182	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers formula the former Prime Minister adopted which started an upward trend that even the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has not been able to curb.
It is a long year since the Prime Minister was elected on the slogan, "the just society". People are beginning to realize what "just society" means. It means squeeze some more. The other day the Prime Minister said to the press, "take a bath". I say to him and to his government that it is time this government took a cold shower to enable them to face up to some of the cold realities and practicalities confronting this nation. Surely it will not be long before other ministers resign if they are responsible and honest and have the kind of integrity of other ministers who served other great Liberal governments and had the courage to resign. The Minister of Agriculture cannot say he is against a boycott because it is bad, for that is the only policy which the government has put forward. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs says he is for a boycott. The Prime Minister has to decide between the new father and the Minister of Agriculture. He has to make that decision. One can understand now why the ministers come to the house only on odd days. I have found out why. So they do not have to answer questions and face up to their political and economic responsibilities.
I want to end on this note. This is one of the opposition days. I say to the minister that we have been criticized because of some of our suggestions and because they have not always been positive. I say to the minister that the day the government pirates took away from the official opposition and the other opposition parties the right to control the pursestrings of the nation they gave the opposition the right to say to the government: "Unless you come up with some definite and positive solutions you will get no more of the taxpayers' money to squander on unworkable ideas." When the government changed the rules in that regard they emasculated parliament. When the minister delivered his lecture I am sure he excited the freshmen but not the seniors. There were only ten Liberals in the house listening to him. This state of affairs was brought about by the government when it changed the rules and took away control of the pursestrings from the opposition. We lost our power but we will regain it when public opinion is aroused in the next three years sufficiently to turn the government out of office.
IMr. Woolliams.]

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in this debate because of the need to counteract the impression created by the motion and confirmed in the speeches of the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) and the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) that price stability and inflation are entirely the responsibilities of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford). I have been hearing about beef, but it sounds like boloney, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext: You can afford both.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
It would be doing a disservice to the Canadian people to make them believe, as the motion implies, that price mechanisms are entirely to blame for inflation at the consumer level, and it should be borne in mind that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs limits its activities in connection with inflation solely to a consideration of price mechanisms.
Therefore, to draw attention to some of the profound factors responsible for the very serious and dangerous inflationary trends in the last few months, I am compelled to broaden the context of the debate. I do so
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
with some diffidence because I am not an economist. What I wish to do in the very few minutes I have is to review the traditional government tools for dealing with inflation in the context of the very peculiar type of inflation which we are experiencing in the marketplace today.
One could say that times are very good today, but the question I want to consider is one which is perhaps on the lips of or coming to the lips of more and more Canadians who participate in our economic life. That question is: If things are so good, how come things are so bad? This is the paradox that dominates economic life today, and it is no exaggeration to say that a growing number of people in this country are getting scared. The weak in our society, old age pensioners, retired public servants, veterans, and people who have saved to arrange for comfortable retirements-the people that I meet every day in my riding-are getting scared. But they are not the only ones. The rich, the strong, the captains of industry, our largest corporations, our municipalities, and people with vast resources of credit are scared too. But the paradox is that we have never been better off, that employment levels in most parts of Canada are healthy, that we are in a period of stable progress and growth which has not abated, except in constructive ways, since the war. Expansion proceeds at a record rate, and there are no signs of depression or even of recession on the horizon. The private decisions of thousands of economic planners to proceed now, to expand now, to buy now, in short to spend and to borrow now, contradict any assumption that a recession is even a remote possibility.
Perhaps the most resourceful of the foregoing statements is the last. Let me elaborate on that. If economic planners in our economic community have learned one lesson in the past 25 years is is this: Don't wait for spring, don't wait at all, do it now, buy it now, borrow now. Virtually every private economic decision made since the war to postpone a spending program or to postpone borrowing in the private sector has been proved to be a mistake. This observation does not apply only to business and government but also to family economic decisions. How many young families would not be better oft today if they had bought the home they now need last year or, better yet, two or five years ago even if they did not need it five years ago. Industry is in the same position. Those who waited to expand until their sales market justified it are sorry that they waited.
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
Underlying the popular attitude which I have just described is a deep and wide confidence that there will not be a depression, and a faith that governments have perfected their techniques for maintaining growth, if only in the interests of full employment, and will not permit a recession. Otherwise, if a depression or a recession were expected, it would pay people to wait before making their big commitments. More private decisions to wait would take the steam out of the economy and if this were to happen, inflation would be curbed. But because people believe the opposite, that is, that inflation will continue and that there will be growth, and act accordingly, we are faced with an economy in which the risk of loss in an enterprise is completely discounted. If growth is assured, there will be no losses, and there are no risks in expansion, even premature expansion.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I submit that not enough thought has been given to the facts of life, the conventional approaches, as they apply to an economy where there is this new underlying confidence. All past economic policy becomes questionable because it was based on a system in which decision-makers were prepared to face the possibility of declining prices and shrinking markets. These are alternatives which imply advantages in consolidation and in delaying commitments. People no longer think this way.
I should like to review the traditional solutions which are being applied to this new form of inflation. There are three standard and traditional government techniques. First, there is fiscal policy. How does fiscal policy apply under these new assumptions? In the case of fiscal policy one can see there should be no change; the proper tax response to a boom, to a "demand-pull" inflation, would be to raise taxes, reduce expenditures and seek balanced budgets. This forces economic decision-makers in the private sector to wait, if only by reducing their means to proceed through taxation.
A second traditional device for controlling inflation is that which is associated with the government's role as a consumer. When private demand increases and prices rise, it is still appropriate even under the new assumptions, as under the old system, for the government to reduce its demands for goods and services.
10104	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16. 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
But when it comes to the third aspect of these control devices, that of monetary control, there is a striking difference. I should like to elaborate on this. Under the new assumptions, the old monetary policy is totally wrong; in fact, it does the opposite of what is required. Traditionally, the government gets the Bank of Canada to raise the interest rate hoping in this way to deter people from expanding, on the theory that businessmen do not want to assume the risk of high fixed costs of interest, particularly over long periods of time. In the past they knew that if they borrowed at high rates and their competitors were able, after waiting, to borrow at lower rates, their competitors would be able to undersell them. It seems clear, however, that this type of reasoning has become obsolete. People feel they are taking no real risk by paying high interest rates because they are confident there will be no depression or recession tomorrow-that prices will be high enough and markets broad enough to support their high costs. This knowledge or belief arises because it is felt that the government's control over the economy and its dedication to the goal of full employment implies such consequences.
If I am correct in this observation, Mr. Speaker, it follows that raising the interest rate in these circumstances has no effect in reducing inflation, and does not curb borrowing. Rather, as I see it, it increases inflation. If interest rates were lower, and if high taxes and reduced government spending were maintained as policies, I submit we should experience less inflation than we are seeing today. Higher interest rates are causing inflation; they are themselves inflationary. Such, at any rate, is the undeniable conclusion one must draw from all the fiddling with interest rates which has taken place from late 1957 until the one per cent increase of last week by the Federal Reserve Board. Possibly a usurious increase of the sort which took place last week-an extreme increase-will take effect in a way in which mild and moderate increases have failed to take effect in the last ten years.
It is not said often enough or clearly enough that Canada does not and cannot have an independent interest policy. Our interest policy is the United States interest policy. I am not proud of this, but my feelings on the matter and the feelings of other Canadians do not affect the question at all. In the growing and important debate on foreign ownership and its effect on Canada, much has been said
EMr. Kaplan.]
about our inability to control our economy. I reject this criticism, not totally, but when it is made on a holistic basis.
The present occasion is perhaps not one on which to discuss the broad subject of the high input or, to be precise, the high United States input into our own economic system, but in order to deal with the topic of inflation, as I have been doing, I must refer to the serious political problems which Americans face, problems which have resulted in what I regard as a counterproductive interest rate policy.
Like ourselves, the Americans deal with inflation in their economy by regulating government spending, by the use of tax devices and by means of an interest policy. The Americans have been unable to control government spending to the extent we have been able to do. In Canada we have been much more successful. Of course, they have two wars to fight, one in Viet Nam and the other in their cities, and these take a toll. This leaves the Americans with only two devices- the taxing power and control over the interest rate.
Under our system of cabinet government and majority control the government can, in practice, impose taxes at will in the interest of combatting inflation. In this respect I believe the Canadian government has done its duty even to the point of pain. But the United States government has no comparable straightforward procedure for implementing tax policies, however urgent. Last week, for example, the United States administration sent to the house ways and means committee six former secretaries of the treasury to make a bipartisan appeal for the retention of the income surtax. Yet today there is still no assurance that its efforts in this regard will succeed. It is obviously most difficult for the United States government to rely on tax policies or on tax proposals to control inflation. It is therefore left with its power to control the interest rate. I believe it is this uncertainly about tax proposals which has led the administration to rely too heavily on measures of the Federal Reserve Board intended to fill the breach arising where reduced public spending and increased taxation are not available. Monetary policies alone, however, cannot control inflation and these efforts in the United States have injured the economy of that country and are injuring our own economy. As I suggested earlier, they have backfired and high interest rates have become an inflationary factor.
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
I have a few minutes left, Mr. Speaker, and in these few minutes I should like to consider the responsibility of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I have argued that there are weaknesses in the traditional devices used to control inflation. I have suggested, without taking the opportunity in this debate to elaborate, that there is little one can do to ensure the success of an independent interest policy in this country at present; there is nothing we could do, assuming we want to maintain the present rate of influx of foreign capital and the present rate of economic growth.
One suggestion was attributed to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). It was that the government ought to try the approach of putting out guidelines. Guidelines, in a few words, involve picking a rate out of thin air, or one arrived at after study, and declaring that all good citizens are required to forgo increases of more than, say, 6 per cent in any one year. This sounds as though it might work, but the fact is it was tried in this country a few years ago and found to be unsuccessful. Guidelines are taken by people in today's economy to represent the minimum advances permissible. If the guideline is set at 6 per cent, for instance, a manufacturer feels he is not doing his duty if he does not raise his prices by 6 per cent. Similarly, a union feels it is entitled to an increase of 6 per cent and begins bargaining on the basis of that 6 per cent. Guidelines are too simplistic, and I hope the suggestion I mention has been incorrectly imputed to the Leader of the Opposition. We have had experience with guidelines and found that they are inflationary in themselves.
Earlier in my remarks I referred to the feeling among buyers and borrowers that no depression or recession is likely. This is supplemented by a conviction people have today that inflation will continue, that prices will continue to rise. This in itself disturbs the mechanism of the marketplace. Despite the fact that there is still some slack in the economy, some unused capacity, and adequate supplies of most goods and services, people have learned to consider the marketplace unfair, a futile place in which to bargain. It is into this area that the new Prices and Incomes Commission has been launched to try to give the public the information it requires to offer resistance to prices that are not justified by an underlying cost push. This is not a superficial matter; neither is it an easy task. It is an approach that requires study in depth.
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers [DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
The hon. member for Calgary North suggested that the commission can stop price increases. The matter is not as easy as that. The commission must go behind an increase to demonstrate it is not justified by a cost push and analyse the cost of the product, employees' salaries, tax increases and rising transportation costs. All these factors have to be considered. The government cannot be expected to develop its policies, as the hon. member for Calgary North does, by reading newspapers and advertisements. Surely to be credible as a force the commission has to know what it is talking about. The commission has been slow in starting. It is beginning to study a new field. But I must say, in conclusion, that I am not yet prepared to write off its efforts, and I wish it well.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset I believe it is a fair statement to say that the minister shares with all Canadians great concern at the high cost of living. However, I must go further and point out that showing concern about a problem and doing something about it are two different things.
I class the minister as one of my personal friends. I have known him for many years. May I take this opportunity to offer Mrs. Bas-ford and the minister my sincere congratulations on the increase in their family.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
I have had a great deal of admiration for the minister through the years, having worked with him for three years at least on the joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate that investigated the high cost of living.
In my opinion the Department of Consumer Affairs has been touted as a palliative to Canadian consumers, but as far as having a restraining influence on prices is concerned its effect has been nil. I go further and say that this is not exactly the fault of the Department of Consumer Affairs, far from it. The fact that the government of which the minister is a member has mismanaged the economy of the country has been very effective in driving up the cost of living, and all the consumer and corporate affairs departments in the world would be unable to rectify the situation. Everything has got out of bounds, and much of the distress can be attributed to the complete unawareness of the government of the factors contributing to the
10186	COMMONS DEBATES	June 1G. 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers type of inflation we are now caught up in. Indeed, this belief was expanded on by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) who has just resumed his seat, and may I congratulate him on a very thoughtful speech.
It seems to me that the government has regarded inflation with one eye on the old textbook description of inflation-too much money chasing too few goods. It is obvious to all of us in this chamber, this tremendous group gathered here between five and six each night, that this is not the type of inflation from which we are suffering. If you have the money in Canada today, Mr. Speaker, you can buy anything you set your heart on. I repeat-if you have the money.
The cause of our distress today can be blamed in large measure on world conditions and on a government that failed to recognize the danger signals and do something about the problem long ago. We members of parliament, led by the Liberal government, removed the ceiling on bank interest rates some time ago, with disastrous effects that we see all around us today. The banks really needed that measure. The financial statements of the chartered banks show that profit levels are up 30 to 35 per cent. Government spending has continued at very high levels, with continuing government demands on the money market helping to bring about interest rates that are prohibitive. This in turn has driven up the cost of buying goods, renting houses, and everything else.
In addition, the government continues to increase taxes, which in turn has the effect of increasing prices right down the line. Labour has had no recourse but to ask for more money. The net effect of labour's demands has resulted in purchasing power remaining constant, because each increase in wages has brought with it an increase in the cost of goods. It is a vicious circle, like a dog chasing his tail.
Therefore, in order to pacify those whose complaints about the cost of living have been vociferous and to offer them something by way of meeting their demands for a halt to the ever-escalating cost of living, what has the government done? A government that is sterile of ideas did the obvious; it brought in a new department. This was a simple way of trying to take off the pressure, since the government had nothing concrete to offer in the form of a solution to this serious problem.
I should like to know what we have received for the $16 million expended thus 
far. The minister had the effrontery to suggest in his remarks today that the house had rushed through his estimates. This is another example of the government's modus operandi. It brings in the estimates of suspect departments on the very last day available under the allocation of time for supply.
One thing we do have is Box 99, about which the minister speaks quite a lot.

speechtext:
I am delighted to hear that, because I was just about to say, in fairness, that there have been a few convictions, though chiefly in regard to false and misleading advertising claims. This is all to the good; there is no complaint at all in this regard. However, the department will have to show the house something more tangible than that in the near future if we can ever hope to justify the department's expenditure.
As I mentioned earlier, the people of Canada have had to seek increased salaries and wages just to keep up with the cost of living, though in some instances this has been difficult to accomplish. However, there is one exception in the long list of increases, and that is the percentage of one's income required to be spent on food. This percentage has shown a reduction almost continuously since world war II. In the years prior to world war II the food requirements of the average family in Canada cost in excess of 30 per cent of that family's total wage or salary. As I say, this percentage has steadily declined, with rare temporary interruptions in the decline, until today the food budget of the average family is approximately 19 to 20 per cent of the take-home pay. I am not suggesting for one minute that we should reverse this trend, but I do suggest that it is a factor to keep in mind.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
What are we getting for our $16 million? I represent an area in Canada that is noted for beef cattle finishing feed lots. It was of great interest to me to find out what was going on in the beef business. To be fair, you cannot take isolated cases. You need the whole picture. Where would a person normally expect
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
to get that type of information? I wanted to get an answer to what I thought was a reasonable question, namely, what was the average price of beef in supermarkets across Canada in 1968 compared with the prices today, and were any discernable trends developing?
One would expect to receive this type of information from the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, provided one had not forgotten the debate which took place when this department was established. That is exactly what I had done, forgotten these debates. I should have remembered this was just a Liberal government proliferation of departments. I should have remembered it was a department without teeth-like me.

speechtext: You were on the committee that recommended it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
I am sure hon. members are interested in knowing how I made out. Seven phone calls between 10.12 and 10.30 got me the following replies: Six responses "unavailable at the moment, he or she should be back about 11; in the meantime, for the information you want you should phone such and such a number".
I remember being on the committee. I remember a very bright, intelligent lady in the consumer business, Miss Ordway. When I telephoned her office, I was told she was busy on another line and I could not disurb her. I persevered and finally on one of my phone calls I was given the following information by a young lady: "We have no information on comparative prices, perhaps you can get your information from D.B.S. or the Department of Agriculture". I was also told "Professor Young might compile this type of information, but probably not because he will just specialize in trends". I say that Professor Young has his work cut out for him, because it looks as if the whole department is going to revolve around him.
I am prepared to give the minister and his department all the time they need, but they better start cutting the mustard soon in order to justify the expenditures involved in this department. I say to the housewives allied against soaring prices and all the consumer groups who are protesting against the high cost of living, don't get your hopes too high that the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will, or for that matter can do much for you. I predict the department's biggest contribution will be to take $16 million more tax dollars.
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
I did not give up because I wanted to get some relative figures on the retail prices of beef in 1968 compared with today. I got in touch with D.B.S. and received the following information. Last year on the Toronto market, which is Ontario's largest, the wholesale price of dressed beef averaged 50.8 cents per pound. This price is the equivalent of 1,050 to 1,150 pounds of live weight cattle, bringing on the average in that same market $28 to $29 per hundredweight, with the odd top grade going as high as $31 per hundredweight. Recently, the price has moved up to as high as $37 and $38 per hundredweight. This indicates an increase of 22 per cent to 24 per cent in the price to the producer. Since that peak, the price has dropped off $1 to $2 per hundredweight and as of this morning the price on the Toronto Cattle Market is $35 to $36 for the above mentioned type.
The question then is why did the price of beef go up and why will it not drop too much? The reason I received from D.B.S. is that the cattle population in Canada in 1968 was only 98 per cent of the 1967 total, yet the human population of Canada grew by several percentage points. In other words, there are not as many cattle in the country. As the minister said the other night and repeated today in the house, supply and demand rules the market. I would be the first to admit that figures are misleading. The number of cattle in Canada does not tell the whole story. The number of cattle ready for market tells the story, and this is where we are short.
I received the following figures from D.B.S. this morning. They show the average retail prices across Canada for May, 1968 and May, 1969 and reported telephone prices from meat departments in stores in the city of Ottawa as of this morning. Sirloin steak, May, 1968, $1.18; 1969, $1.39 and today in the Ottawa supermarkets, $1.69; round steak, May, 1968, $1.06; May, 1969, $1.21 and today, $1.39; rolled rib roast, May, 1968, $1.04; May, 1969, $1.13 and today $2. These prices are being charged today in the chain stores in the city of Ottawa.

speechtext:
There is something funny going on! These prices indicate two things to me, Mr. Speaker. First, the producers have finally received a long overdue increase in their prices. Second, using the figures of May, 1968 and May, 1969, the increase is pretty much in keeping with other increases in the
10188	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16. 1966
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers cost of living. However, the prices being charged in Ottawa chain stores today, compared with past averages, is something else again. I question if prices will decline very much in the near future in spite of the minister's unqualified support of a certain supermarket head. This gentleman's advice to housewives to boycott high beef prices does not impress me as much as it obviously impressed the minister.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Two weeks before this gentleman made his pronouncement I happened to be in a livestock broker's office when he slammed the phone down in disgust. I asked, "What was all that about"? He replied, "The chains have just left the market; they are going to boycott the Toronto market." I do not know whether the company owned by the minister's friend formed one of those chains or not, but as they are leaders in the field I suspect they probably did. As I say, this was prior to this gentleman's appeal to the ladies to conduct a boycott. As Shakespeare said, "Methinks he doth protest too much." But, Mr. Speaker, it may be good for politics. Perhaps the minister's friend may decide to go into politics in Toronto, as has been suggested by a certain senator from that area.
Today choice cattle in Toronto are selling at $35 to $36. Comparable grade cattle are selling in Chicago at $35. The live price of Canadian cattle needs to drop only $1 per hundredweight and then it will be feasible to export Canadian beef to that midwestern market. There are added costs in exporting from Ontario to Chicago as compared with marketing in Toronto. First, there is $1.50 per hundredweight duty. Then, there is 70 cents per hundredweight extra freight costs, and about 50 cents per hundredweight for extra shrink. But there is a plus factor of exchange on money of 1\ per cent so that cattle, particularly in Ontario, can and will go to the U.S. if the Canadian price declines as little as $1 per hundredweight.
I strongly suggest to the minister that he and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) try to get on the same team because I think there is very little that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) can do about this situation. The Minister of Agriculture hit the nail on the head when he said:
Past prices were not high enough to attract enough money into the expansion of beef production, so prices are starting to rise this year because demand is growing faster than supply.
IMr. McCutcheon.]
The minister also emphasized the fact that Canadian consumers would be well advised not to try a boycott. He pointed out that if more farmers were forced out of beef production, then the consumer would ultimately have to pay an awful lot more money for meat. I suggest that the housewives, the buyers of beef, can do an awful lot. I was interested to hear the minister's advice to housewives today. Supermarkets and butcher shops are in a quandary trying to sell meat.-

Indeed, on many of the items I do agree with the minister. I was just about to speak of the customer who goes to the store and says to the butcher, "There is too much fat on that piece of beef. I don't want to have to pay for all that fat." But chain stores and other buyers of meat will not accept an animal from the producer unless it does have some fat on it. When all the fat is removed it automatically increases the price of the product.
I suggest to consumers that they should keep the pressure on, but they should apply it to the government to cut down on its profligate spending, so that taxes can be reduced as well as the high cost of money. In my opinion, these things have contributed more to the high cost of living than the increase in the price of food.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was much encouraged when the minister rose today to say he was highly sensitive to the problem of inflation, particularly when he emphasized its effect on the poor, and more especially on those in the categories of pensioners and unorganized workers. I found his expression of concern, grounds for optimism. I thought he might be about to announce some new, startling and
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
imaginative program to deal with the problems that these people face. But instead we got a rehash of the same thing we have heard in this house for many months, with nothing new whatsoever.
If he and his government had been concerned with the problem you would have thought he would have done something to deal with the unorganized workers, the regionally impoverished workers, the persons living on pensions. You would have thought the government would have implemented the Woods report recommendations dealing with veterans pensions. But no, the government has waited over a year and done nothing with respect to that report. You would have thought the government would have been concerned about retired civil servants living impoverished lives. But no, it has not acted to increase the pensions of retired civil servants. The Canada Pension Plan, in which there is a wonderful 2 per cent escalator clause, is absolutely useless in an economy which has an annual inflation rate averaging four per cent. Even with a 2 per cent pension increment, the people receiving it must live at a 2 per cent lower standard of living.
You would have thought that the government, dissatisfied with a winter works program which had some faults and there is no doubt about that, would have revised that program; made it more imaginative and expanded it. But no, the government scrapped the winter works program. Again you would have thought that the government of one of the few countries in the industrialized world which in the last 10 years had an average unemployment rate of around 5 per cent-and some 40 per cent to 45 per cent of Canada's unemployed are located in Quebec alone-would have adopted a crash program to deal with unemployment. But of course, we have nothing like that.
On paper we have a very good program to deal with regional economic disparities, but in the current budget only a few paltry millions of dollars are devoted to it. You would have thought the Watkins report recommendations would have been dealt with in some meaningful way by the government, but again we have seen no action. Instead, what do we get? We have had a series of measures which reveal the Herbert Hoover mentality of the government. The solution favoured by the government is one which has been favoured by governments for some 30 years, that is to have sound fiscal and monetary policies.
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers [DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
What does this mean? It means, of course, an effort to cut down wherever possible in the public sector of the economy. We receive little homilies from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs day in and day out on this. I should like to make two points on this issue. First of all, if we are concerned at times in the short run about inflation and if we do want to cut back on investment expansion, why must we always concentrate on the public sector? Why are no selective cut-backs in force in the private sector of the economy? Do we need more office buildings which cost millions of dollars in Montreal or in any other city? Do we need more gas stations? Do we not need in fact some control over the sector of private income which selects investments when we decide to cut back to deal with inflation? Some people think we should not cut back when there is a need for houses. They believe that we should perhaps pour millions of dollars as directly as possible into a corporation which would be responsible for housing. But a government so committed ideologically to a privately dominated and privately run economy can think of cutting back in only the public sector. Such a government then has the nerve, in my judgment, to go to the public and say it is doing the public a favour when in reality it is cutting back on funds for housing, hospitals and schools in an already impoverished public sector of the economy.
I should like to leave that point because, although I believe it is important, I do not think the principal method of dealing with inflation should be this kind of selective action with a bias in favour of private interests and against government initiative in creating a fully employed work force. We need an expanding and efficient economy. In short, we should have had white papers which contained policies for full employment. To my knowledge, never in the history of this country have we had such white papers. We receive papers such as the one concerned with policies on prices, or whatever it was, which we received just before the new year.
What should be done? I think we should quit fooling around with meat prices and items of this sort. What we should be concerned with is developing an economy which is as independent as it possibly can be in a modern interdependent world. This means we must free ourselves from the overwhelming influence of the United States economy. We
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers cannot deal in a meaningful way in Canada with interest rates when these are connected through the general economic structure with the interest rates in the United States. Over a 10 or 15 years period we must break the nature of our branch plant economy and create an independent, Canadian owned efficient industrial economy. I spoke at length during an earlier session of this parliament and therefore shall not take much more of parliament's time at this moment in suggesting the ways in which this should be done. The leader of my party and the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) in a recent debate elaborated on policies which would be very important for this country in this regard.
There is one item which I think might be mentioned, especially if we compare it with the many small efforts which are being carried out by the minister's department. If I had to choose at this point, I would say we should reduce that department's budget to $1 and all the funds which are allocated to that department should be put into a Crown research and development corporation. If primarily we are concerned about a research institution, why do we not in this country develop a pool of talent which would be available to private and public enterprises. Such a research and development corporation would be able to make recommendations about development of industry in Canada based on our resources both physical and human. This would lead to an efficient, competitive economy in the international market. We have never dealt with this point seriously. It has always been pooh-poohed as some ivory tower scheme. As I mentioned previously Japan, the Scandinavian countries and the Netherlands have committed themselves to precisely this kind of policy over an extended number of years. It is not an ivory tower scheme at all. It would involve some serious structural changes and the serious spending of money on research and development in this country.
I should like to leave this part of my speech and move on to a comment about the Prices and Incomes Commission. I was pleased that today the minister did not leave us with any grand illusions about the ultimate efficacy of this commission. His previous statement provided no ground for optimism on this score. I believe he has decided to back down a bit and talk more about the monetary and fiscal policy dealing with inflation rather than the Prices and Incomes Commission. I think perhaps he has found out that in this 
June 16, 1969
country there is very little confidence, especially among professional economists, in this Prices and Incomes Commission. I ask the minister why he has not been able to fill the vacant positions on this commission? When are the two commissioners to be appointed? I wonder whether part of the difficulty is that the academic community, to name one part of the community, is entirely disenchanted with the "academic" commissions established by this government. They have seen what has happened in respect of the Carter Commission report and the Watkins Commission report, as well as others.
I suggest in all seriousness that there is little intellectual respect among those professionally concerned with economic matters for the intentions of this government. Particularly among economists who have a genuine social concern about this country, I have heard the view expressed-and I imagine the minister has also heard this view expressed- that the net effect of this Prices and Incomes Commission is likely to be a negative one. I think the minister suggested himself that he is aware of this. If we do have publicly revealed statements about general trends in wages, for example, who is likely to be affected? The minister suggested that the private sector of the economy, the management level or the oligopolistic level in this country will not pay much attention to it. They will set their prices as they always have. They are quite unconcerned about whatever guidelines might be established. So, basically, are the powerful trade unions. They will be as successful as they have been in bargaining or at least will not be greatly affected. They will be affected, if anyone is to be affected by this Prices and Incomes Commission-

I should like to thank my colleagues in the house and I promise I will be very brief.
What I was going to suggest is that the only groups who will be seriously affected by public revelation of prices, incomes and

June 16, 1969	COMMONS
income trends in the country will be the unorganized and the weak. Those recommendations or guideline statements will be used to keep down the wages of those who are already in an unfortunate position in terms of bargaining strength. Hospital workers, unorganized workers and civil servants will be forced to remain at their low level of wages.
Therefore, like many professional economists, I have little faith at all in the ultimate effect of this Prices and Incomes Commission.
I have been brief and I think I have made one or two constructive suggestions, the details of which have been elaborated by me and other spokesmen of my party earlier during this session. What I think is most important for us to keep in mind is that this government espouses a concern for the unemployed and those on fixed incomes but is still talking in terms of ideas that were outmoded in the 1930's. The government is either incompetent or unconcerned, and on neither ground should it go before the Canadian people with any degree of confidence in terms of its actions.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I had not meant to speak on this motion, but I find myself drawn into the debate because of a difference of opinion with some of the previous speakers. In opening, may I say a few words with respect to remarks made by two earlier speakers. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) purported to give the count of Liberal members in the house. I differ with him in that count; I believe he overlooked counting the Liberals on the east side of the chamber. The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) mentioned the high price of steak in that city and indicated that he suspected a price fixing or monopoly. He did not bring forth any evidence of price fixing or a monopoly-

nor was there any suggestion that all the stores, or even two stores,
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers sold steak at the same price. There is no indication that any housewife has complained that she suspects price fixing or a monopoly, nor is there any suggestion that the small butcher's shops are in cahoots with the large stores to maintain the high price of steak. In any event, I would say to him and the people of his riding that if there is any such evidence and the people bring it forward, I am confident that the Director of Research and Investigation under the Combines Investigation Act will take prompt action.
I agree that the price of food, clothing and living accommodation is too high; there is no question about that. I also agree that each Canadian would like to see his own income go up and at the same time prices remain stable for all goods and services. Obviously, this cannot be. We must look for some other solution. Let us first examine the high cost of rental accommodation. Surely, we must accept the fact that rent is determined by the selling price of accommodation, that is, the selling price of a home or condominium unit. Then, why are these prices so high? There are five basic elements: there is the high cost of financing, the high cost of land available for development, the high taxation which places the full expense load for education on the municipality, archaic zoning provisions, and high construction costs.
The task force heard representations from all parts of Canada. They considered these matters and made recommendations. Within days the government introduced the new housing bill, and I suggest it covered everything within the jurisdiction of this Parliament. Although much has been said about the high cost of financing, we are living in a dream world if we do not accept the fact that high interest rates in this country are substantially controlled by the interest rates of the United States. The interest rate in that country now exceeds 8 per cent, and unless our interest rates are higher our money will be drained off immediately.
During the last seven or eight years land ready for development in the Toronto area has increased in price by about 300 per cent. Something should be done, but the solutions lie completely within the jurisdiction of the provinces. In respect of planning and taxation I point out that whereas 50, 60 or 70 years ago, when Toronto had a population of not more than 200,000, we built attractive, semidetached houses on 20-foot lots. Many streets of such houses are still there to be seen. Today, almost every municipality demands a
10192	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers 50, 55 or 60-foot lot and a large house in order to provide a tax base to pay for the educational costs.
This type of planning is now out of date and should be changed by the province. If not, we will have immensely stretched-out cities with transportation nightmares, and parents taking one to two hours to get home to their children after a day's work. The province should change these zoning provisions to allow more flexibility for high-rise apartments, some 20 or 25-foot lots, and mobile home parks. The basis of taxation should be changed so that a municipality may allow homes to be built on lots of this size without impairing its ability to provide education. But perhaps the most important and urgent matter today is the high cost of construction. Today, it is considered modest to ask for a 15 per cent incease in wages or salaries over a two-year period. This attitude is now almost chronic. But a 15 per cent increase in a two-year period is a 30 per cent increase in a four-year period. When one considers the increase upon increase, let us say it is a 50 per cent increase in a six-year period. We cannot increase wages by 50 per cent in six years and not cause continuing inflation. The hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon) said that unions have no option but to make these demands. I ask, what about the construction unions? They make no such modest demands. There, the wage rates of the trades vary from $6 to $8.50 an hour, which produces for them an annual income greater than that of a member of parliament and of some professional people who took years to prepare for their profession. In addition, usually the member of parliament and the professional people work considerably longer hours.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The construction unions have taken a stranglehold on Canadian housing, and with their monopoly they are driving up the cost of living for every Canadian at a fantastic rate. Whereas in the United States in 1962, construction workers increased their hourly rate by about 12 cents an hour, the increase now is from 50 cents to 75 cents an hour. Recently such a strike was settled in Toronto at $1.71 an hour, over a two year period, plus considerable fringe benefits. This would amount to something between 85 cents and one dollar an hour. We ask ourselves: Can a teacher on $7,000 a year or a clerk on $3,000 afford the luxury of their services? The payment of 
DEBATES	June 18, 1969
these exorbitant wages not only drives up the cost of construction but, in addition, increases the price of goods. Factories have to be built and these service people are on the staff. The effect of these wage increases are also indirectly reflected in our economy and thus upon our cost of living as well causing the spiralling inflation. In addition, the action of these people sets a precedent. Other labour groups must, for their own self-preservation, demand substantial increases to have any hope of hiring the services of these trades.
I do not question the right to strike. It has done much to improve the living standards of many. But in some cases the power is too great, and recently it has been exercised without responsibility. I do not quarrel with the individual seeking gain, but sometimes he does not gain. If he is on strike for six or eight weeks, the increase he gets usually just compensates him for the time he lost his income. The people who gain are the union organisers. They become important on T.V.
I say to each member of this house: Just imagine what the price of food would be if farmers should ever be paid at the same rate as these construction people. Let us take it further, and suppose that we increase proportionately the wages of all those who process the food between the farm and the final sale to the consumer. No doubt, in order to keep rents down some may recommend rental control, but I do not think logic would allow us to consider rent control unless all prices and all incomes were fixed. Surely, each of us want to see that only as a last resort.
What has the government done? We have cut back on government spending; we have discouraged commercial building and we have balanced the budget. The minister has appointed an advisory council of experts to advise him constantly as to what can be done. At this point we must warn the public to stop purchasing and to save and invest some of their money to slow down the heated economy. Secondly, we must warn some of these people who make excessive demands that if they keep it up, and the spiral is allowed to speed up, we will get to the point at which no one will be able to afford their services. If it does keep up ones insurance and ones pension will be completely eroded away-in fact the whole life insurance industry will be destroyed.
Personally, I do not care about the fact that the price of beefsteak has become so high. I have literally felt embarrassed at the price for which one can buy chicken and turkey,
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
and I wonder how the producers live. I would not consider it too great a hardship to live on chicken and turkey for a while instead of beef.
May I say in conclusion that this is a real problem with which we must grapple and which we must solve, but this is something that all Canadian people must feel and on which they must co-operate. The minister has done all he can at the moment, but if we do not get some co-operation with respect to these wage demands, we may have no alternative at some point in the future but to fix rentals, prices and wages.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
First, I should like to congratulate the minister on his and Mrs. Basford's addition to the family of little Master Basford. I think it is quite commendable, and we on this side are looking forward to those 5 cent cigars.
Never have I listened to such arrogance and conceit as I have listened to today from the minister who claims that he is highly sensitive to the poor who, he claims, are unable to talk for themselves and who cannot protect themselves against higher prices. This is why this motion is particularly appropriate at a time when the cost of living weighs heavily on every Canadian. It is particularly appropriate at a time when the government has demonstrated a complete lack of interest in the fate of ordinary Canadians forced to pay more and more for less and less. It is appropriate at a time when Canadians are forced to run harder and harder to stay where they were a year or two years ago. The costs borne by the consumer, the householder, the homemaker and the salaried wage earner have gone up and up, while salaries have not kept pace. Nobody knows this better than the minister. Nobody cares less than the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
What is the use of this kind of motion? Is it going to produce any action from the government? I doubt it. The government must know what the situation is. They have been told about it for the past three years. We have been telling them about it and so have other opposition parties. In the face of high interest rates, prices that are way out of line, rising costs, and increased competition from abroad, the government has shown a total lack of interest. In the face of an increase in consumer prices of something in the nature of 14 per cent in the past three years, the government has done little to show its awareness of the problem.
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
We have had a Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. It was established with tremendous fanfare. With equal fanfare the minister set up a committee before which there was a parade of witnesses, each of whom disclaimed any responsibility for what is happening. Somebody somewhere is taking a rake-off. The minister was not able to establish who it was. Surely, the minister cannot pretend that his department has been a success. The facts and figures speak for themselves. We have seen the greatest increases in prices and costs in Canada's peacetime history. This speaks for itself. The minister cannot show that his department has been instrumental in saving the consumer a single penny. He certainly cannot demonstrate that his department has been instrumental in holding down prices. If he had done so effectively, Canadian consumers would not find themselves in their present position.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
As one surveys the whole spectrum of price and cost increases, one finds there is hardly an area in which consumers are not obliged to pay a great deal more now than they did when this government came to office. The tragedy is not that the government has failed to take action, the real tragedy is that the government doesn't give a damn.
Never were truer words spoken than those uttered by the former minister of transport (Mr. Hellyer) when he said, with a great light dawning, that this government was incapable of dealing with the nuts and bolts issues. I do not intend to repeat at length his great panegyric, one which gained the admiration of thinking people everywhere, but in the course of it he placed an expert finger on the real weakness of the government. It began as a government divorced from the people. It is now a government divorced from reality. It is a government which has occupied its time and the time of this house chasing the will-o-the-wisp of medico-socio tinkering while the people who voted it into power could not make ends meet.
Last week, while interest rates took another giant step upward with the full approval of the government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) was prepared to carve up the constitution like a chicken and hand it trussed up on a plate to Ontario and Quebec. Only a couple of weeks ago the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) brought down a theoretical budget which continued the iniquitous 3 per cent surtax and placed a freeze on development in
10194	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16, 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers western Canada. Hon. members opposite know this to be the case. They produced a plastic budget to go along with the new plastic constitution and now they expect us to bow down and tell them how great they are.
While the government is obsessed with prefabricated prophesies dreamed up in the back rooms of the Liberal party, Canadians are becoming fed up with the way in which basic issues are ignored and neglected. A great number of people are leaving the Prime Minister-the number is rapidly reaching the proportion of an exodus. There was the minister of transport. He gave us, as his reason, that the government was not dealing with the real problems. There will not be much disagreement about that. Then, there were two of the Senatorial pillars of the Liberal establishment, Senators Lang and Aird, who left in disgust at the pussyfooting in connection with our NATO obligations. This proves conscience can exist in the other place. Now, we find the Stanburys getting restless.

speechtext:
The gentleman in the other place. When members of the government's strategy board in the other place get fed up, things have to be really bad. This is the stage which has been reached as we come to deal with the present motion, one which simply opens up a corner of the general disarray and inertia of which the government has been guilty. As an example of the administration talking out of both sides of its mouth at the same time, we find the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) urging consumers to boycott beef while the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) expresses satisfaction over rising prices. I would be the last to disagree with the Minister of Agriculture when he says it is time the farmers got a fair return, and this is especially true in the light of the government's inability to sell wheat. One can understand the hon. gentleman's relief at the prospect of increased income in western Canada. But it is certainly an indication of the ineptness of the government when the only solution the minister in charge of consumer affairs can think of is for consumers to boycott beef which they cannot afford to buy in the first place.
What the minister has failed to deal with to the satisfaction of consumers is the course of events between the time the beef leaves the farmer's hands and the time it is placed, neatly wrapped in cellophane, on meat counters across the nation. Can the minister explain

why the price per pound should increase by 200 per cent between the loading chute and the supermarket counter? The chain stores claim their profit is only 2 per cent, and that is reasonable. Somebody is taking a beating, and it is usually the people at each end of the stick, that is to say, the farmer at one end and the consumer at the other. The Minister of Agriculture feels he has taken care of his end successfully, which leaves the minister in charge of consumer affairs holding the dirty end of the stick. Perhaps that minister should now boycott the Minister of Agriculture.
When the most experienced and far-sighted minister in the government, one holding the senior portfolio of transportation, says the government is not doing a job, we are bound to believe him. I refer to the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Hellyer). What is happening with regard to interest rates, the cost of money and consumer prices all along the line just proves how right the former minister of transport was when he said this government neglects the nuts and bolts issues.
There are a lot of nuts and bolts in government, Mr. Speaker, and I am afraid that in this government there are more nuts than there are bolts. The best thing the government could do to help Canadians everywhere would be to resign.
