respect to him. What I meant was that the resolution merely oversimplifies the problem of increasing prices, really fails to define the problem and offers no solutions whatsoever. The resolution gives the impression that there are panaceas in regard to inflation, that there are magic solutions, that all that a government has to do is more or less to snap its fingers and these problems will go away. Having listened to members of the opposition parties in this debate, it is rather difficult to understand what is being suggested to solve the problems of inflation.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
This afternoon the hon. member for Lamb-ton-Kent (Mr. McCutcheon), I think it was, said that the problem of rising prices was due to the government spending too much money. A member of the New Democratic party, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broad-bent), said he thought we should spend more money in certain areas. This clearly illustrates that there is no simple solution to the problems of inflation. It is also clearly illustrates that the opposition parties have no obvious solutions to meet these problems.
The condemnation of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in this resolution for his failure to protect the Canadian consumer is tantamount to a condemnation of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) because there is still sickness in this country, or a condemnation of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Turner) because there is still crime being committed in Canada. There are many more measures that could be taken, of course, to improve our price situation, but I submit that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has done some extremely important work since he took office last summer.
If we are to measure the minister's effectiveness we might do well to compare the price record in Canada with that of other countries. No doubt this has been done before, but I think we have to keep reminding the opposition parties of it. For example, in the period 1952 to 1968 Canada ranked with the United States in the maintenance of price stability and had the best record when compared to the other western industrialized countries. During this period Canada and the United States had a 1.7 per cent annual rate of increase, compared with Germany with 1.8 per cent; Italy, 3 per cent; The Netherlands, 3.2 per cent; Britain, 3.2 per cent; Sweden, that great socialist paradise, 3.4 per cent; France, 3.5 per cent and Japan 4.0 per cent.

speechtext:
Yearly increase in prices. According to a table in front of me, Canada and the United States had the best record in this regard in the period 1952 to 1968.
In the period 1965 to 1968, a shorter period, our record was not as good as it was in the longer run, but it was still very commendable. During this period the annual increase in prices in Canada was 3.7 per cent, compared with 4.1 per cent for The Netherlands; 4.8 per cent for Sweden and 4.8 per cent for Japan. Germany and Italy were lower than Canada during that period, and the United States had an increase of 3.1 per cent, 0.6 per cent lower than Canada's level. However, our record was still extremely good.
I point this out to show that, if the problems of inflation are as simple and easy to solve as the opposition parties would pretend, then they must be the only experts in the world who have the answers. It seems that the economic advisers of other countries do not have the answers, because if they did their countries would have a better rate than Canada in the matter of price stability. If we really want to assess the record of this government and the minister, we must compare that record with that of others.
The resolution before the house states that the minister and his department have not been doing very much since the minister was appointed last year. I should like to refer to some of the very important things that this department has done. The department was formed a little over a year ago. When this minister took office last summer-

speechtext:
It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that the speeches of hon. members opposite are not as good as their remarks while other people are speaking.
In pointing out some of the difficulties in resolving the problems of inflation and price increases, may I refer to the report of the consumer prices committee which was submitted to this house on April 20, 1967. This report was the product of the committee that was chaired by the present minister and which received, I might say, the unanimous support of all parties in the house at the time.
I should like to refer to a paragraph on page 4 of the report which reads as follows:
Much of the expert testimony of both academic and government economists emphasized that the increase in the cost of living which has been observed in Canada in the recent past is a complex phenomenon. There have been many influences at v/ork and these in turn set up chain reactions which ultimately permeate the economy and have a buoyant influence on particular prices and on the price level in general.
Then, on page 5 there is this paragraph:
This complicated process-
That is the process of price increases and growing inflation.
-is sometimes oversimplified and an attempt made to attribute a general price increase solely to some particular group such as trade unions, business, financiers, farmers, profiteers or even consumers themselves. The evidence presented to your committee did not support any such unsophisticated view. It is instructive to note that the trend of consumer prices in Canada and the United States has exhibited a similar pattern.
This pattern shows that during the same period of time the price level in Canada had a tendency to follow that of the United States. When the consumer prices committee was sitting, it heard from many economists and experts about the causes of price increases

DEBATES	June 16, 1969
and possible solutions. Not one of these economists suggested that the solution lies in price control. When each expert appeared before the committee, we asked him if the solution was price control. Almost unanimously, they replied that if you try to deal with the problem of inflation through price control, you deal with the symptoms and not the cause of the problem. In other words, you will not really solve the problem for the Canadian consumer by controlling a particular price or prices because this will have a chain reaction which will affect production. In the long run, the consumer will either not get the product concerned or the inflationary pressures will be channelled into other products and other areas.
* (8:40 p.m.)
I wish to refer to the fifth Annual Review of the Economic Council of Canada in which they discuss price stability. I recommend to members of the opposition parties that they read this report because in it are several suggestions for dealing with price stability. Most of these suggestions have been taken up by the government, but to my knowledge none of them have been dealt with today by members of the opposition parties. At page 194 of the review dated September, 1968, the Council states:
One of the main themes of that Review was that there is no simple, easy and quick "policy solution" to price and cost instabilities. A wide range of policies must be brought to bear on the problems.
At page 195, the review continues:
After due allowance for the influence of external price and cost changes, over which Canada may have little or no control, and from which we cannot fully insulate ourselves, we suggest that five essential policy elements are needed to achieve the best possible reconciliation of our price stability goal with other basic economic and social goals. These five elements are:
(1)	the "big levers" of demand policies-monetary and fiscal policies;
(2)	an equally important group of supply policies;
(3)	a number of special policies to cope with particular problems;
(4)	greater public knowledge and understanding about prices and costs; and
(5)	trade and tariff policies.
These are the five solutions put forward by the Economic Council of Canada. The first solution relates to monetary and fiscal policies. I suggest the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) and his predecessor in the last two or three budgets made an attempt to deal with inflation through these tools. The record of the Minister of Finance in this respect is as
June 16. 1969	COMMONS
good as that of any other country in the world using monetary and fiscal policies. However, that is not the only solution.
Secondly, the Economic Council states we must have effective supply policies. Under supply policies they refer to greater labour mobility through manpower policies, improvements in productivity, adjustments to technological change and policies to improve regional balance. In the last two or three years, this government and its predecessor have done much to act in all these areas. The manpower mobility and retraining program was set up by the former government under the leadership of the Right Hon. Mr. Pearson. Productivity was given assistance through several pieces of legislation. One of the newest refers not only to productivity, but regional balance. It is the new bill introduced by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) with regard to regional industrial incentives.
Third, the report refers to adjustments to technological change. Here again, some of the manpower policies which have been put forward by the government attempt to deal with these matters. Fourth, the Economic Council has stated that there should be better coordination in federal-provincial fiscal planning. During the last two federal-provincial conferences, and in the meetings of officials between and before these conferences, the government has put forward plans to have a better and more efficient control over federal-provincial programs. The government has stated several times this sort of thing is extremely necessary if we are to control prices and inflation in Canada. Action is being taken on that recommendation as well.
As a fifth recommendation, the Council states there must be more information for the Canadian consumer with respect to the reasons and the causes behind pricing. It suggests that a planning committee on economic affairs of the Senate and House of Commons be established. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) in this past week or so stated it is his intention to set up such a committee very shortly. In his white paper on price policy which he put out at the end of last year, the minister stated his intention to set up such a committee.
The next recommendation, and this is a very important recommendation, states that we should try to deal with inflation and price increases through reduction in tariffs and trade barriers. I do not know whether any of the opposition members have dealt with this
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers matter. It is well known that in the budget brought down just two weeks ago one of the important provisions was a full implementation of the Kennedy round proposals dealing with tariff reductions and doing a,way with trade barriers.
You cannot have it both ways. When the government does things such as establishing a prices commission, reducing tariffs, establishing supply policies and production policies, you cannot criticize them at the time such measures are introduced and two months later in a debate such as this pretend that the government is not doing anything. The opposition parties would be more constructive if they would try to make improvements at the time the legislation is brought forward. All we get on opposition days are litanies of complaints and grievances against the government, but not much constructive advice as to the problem at hand.

I wish to say a few words nevertheless, because I am very interested in the vote of $16 million for this year which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) has to piddle around with. That is a poor choice of words, but that $16 million is supposed to be used by the minister to curtail inflation and bring costs under control.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
I suggest the minister has been doing an excellent job building up his expense account because he has certainly been travelling a lot.
10198	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16, 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers Every other day I read a speech that the minister has made in Vancouver, in Edmonton or in some other part of Canada. In those speeches he has indicated to the consumers, "If you have any problems you come to Papa, and Papa is going to solve all of them." He indicates that with speeches, persuasion and perseverance the cost of living is going to be brought down. This is very good advertising politically, but if some of the branches of the minister's department were to review this kind of advertising perhaps they would find that it falls into the category of false advertising. If one looks at the results of the minister's department for the last year, and I can speak with experience only of that year, one could conclude that most Canadians one would think this is the kind of advertising they see in connection with many cereals. It is to be taken with a grain of salt, or to be taken with a hogshead of salt, to use a good Newfoundland expression.
We can have our study groups, our think-ins, our speeches, and all kinds of appointments to various bodies and, according to the minister, this will do the job eventually. I have one suggestion I could make to the minister. Let him turn over the $16 million to me. I then would give back $15 million to the Treasury Board, become a millionaire and achieve the same results as he has achieved with respect to the cost of living.
In all seriousness, Mr. Speaker, I just cannot agree with the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) who says that there is no problem. I cannot see that things are working well in Canada. I cannot understand how the average Joe, Tom, Dick or Harry in Canada is making a go of it. I cannot see how he can buy enough of the proper food. In so far as the cost of food is concerned, I am not going to explain that to the minister. This has been done adequately and well in this debate already.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot see how the average fellow can get along today in view of the cost of living. According to the papers I have read, the only cost that has gone down has been the cost of toilet paper. Take the cost of clothing. I cannot see how the average person can adequately clothe his family. If he can afford to buy building materials, he cannot afford to have a house constructed. If he happens to need a repair job done on his home, he just cannot pay the carpenter or the plumber.
If the average Joe has a health problem he had better stay sick because he cannot afford to pay the doctor. If he takes part in a government health plan, his taxes will go sky high. If he wants to buy a car, and the average person in Canada cannot afford to buy a car, the first problem he faces is where is he going to get the money? Secondly, if he does get the money how can he afford to pay the interest on the loan?
Then, he is faced with the cost of educating his children. I can give the minister some facts on the costs of education. Further, if the average Joe does get an education, where is he going to get a job in this country? Even the church is saying, "You have to pay more money." The clergy have to go on holidays and they want an extra dollar. Mr. Speaker, all the time I am talking about the average Canadian Joe. If there is a dollar left after he has paid for the necessities of life, and usually there isn't, the government will take it in taxes.
The average Joe used to be able to buy a dozen beer now and then. Following the recent tax increase in Ontario the price of beer went to $5 a case, so he cannot do that. He couldn't afford it in Newfoundland at any time. If he wants to go on holidays, first of all the government taxes hotel costs at 5 per cent or 10 per cent. Then, if he gets to an hotel he cannot afford to tip the waitress enough, and the waitress won't give good service unless she gets a good tip. If he has a television set he can't afford to get it repaired or timed up.
I could continue in this vein and talk about the cost of furniture.
What if the average Canadian Joe is not working? Here, I am talking about 20 per cent of the Canadians who lived in Atlantic Canada last year. In Newfoundland well over 20 per cent of them were unemployed, and in
June 1G, 1969	COMMONS
some parts of Atlantic Canada and in the more rural parts of Newfoundland, over 50 per cent of them were unemployed.
If he is unemployed, is it because he does not want to work or is it because there is no job opportunity for him? I would like the minister to decide this one. But it isn't his problem. He got elected; he doesn't have to worry about these things. I hear all this talk about, "Send your dollars to Care of Canada." Sometimes it makes me wonder.
If the average Joe happens to be unemployed there is just no chance in the world for him to get beyond the level of holding body and soul together. He can forget about education and the other amenities. This is the same guy I was talking about a few minutes ago, whose taxes are so high that he has little alternative but to go on strike or watch his pay cheque go out the government window.
We in the opposition have brought this matter to the attention of the government this year. I look around and see many members who have told the government, "You are taxing the Canadian worker into the ground." Some hon. members across the way say that is the way to bring inflation under control. They say, "Let us put a 3 per cent surcharge on his income tax; let us bring in an indirect taxation policy for all the provinces." This is the great cry I heard from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) today, that we are going to allow the provinces to tax Canadians indirectly. As taxes increase the average man pays another $5, another $10 or another $15. He gets himself in debt to the point where he has difficulty surviving, then he goes on strike. If he gets higher wages, then the government taxes him more. You cannot blame the average Canadian for becoming restless in the Canadian labour market. I see a number of hon. members here who are quite aware of the labour problems.
Am I going to blame the average Canadian for this? I feel like blaming somebody for the high cost of living, but when I see the results of the budget I cannot blame the average Canadian. As a matter of fact, I can only express surprise that he has not gone further.
Now, Mr. Speaker, if I may become a little parochial I will reflect on the position of the average Newfoundland worker today. In Newfoundland his per capita income, believe it or not, is roughtly $1,000 a year, about half of the average income in Ontario. If the average Newfoundlander who has a per capita income of $1,000 has a wife and two children, he will then have $4,000 per year.
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
If you are living in Newfoundland and you make $4,000 a year, you have quite an income. You are perhaps a professional person. You are certainly not the average fisherman because fishermen make $1,000 per family per year. Anyway, this chap makes himself $4,000 per year. Let me explain what the average person can do with that, but let me take another Newfoundlander who is perhaps in the more usual situation in Newfoundland. I refer to the person who, according to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, in February and March, 1969, was working for $62 for a 44.8 hour week. But as a matter of fact he wasn't, because he was out of work at that time. But if he had been working, he would have been making $62.
Now, if he works five months a year he is a lucky Newfoundlander-June, July, August, September and October. If the companies do not close him out before October he is fortunate. That nets him $1,240. Now, if the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mackasey) is not too tough he might be able to sneak in under the unemployment insurance regulations and get another $700, which brings him up to a total of $1,940. There are tens of thousands of people like him in Newfoundland.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)
Let us allow him 27 per cent for housing or let us make it 25 per cent; that is roughly $45 a month for housing. If he owns his own home he can put on clapboards every 25 years. If not he, has a place for $45 a month equivalent to the average Toronto outhouse if they still have them there. They don't-all right. In other words, he does not have a place to live. I am talking about an O'Brien when I am talking about an average Newfoundlander. Let us allow him 20 per cent for food. That is $25 a month or enough for two T-bone steaks at the Red Line restaurant for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. We will allow him 15 per cent for clothing. That is enough for sneaker boots for his family if he has a gymnasium, but probably there would not be one at the school. Let us allow him 10 per cent for education, or about, $10 a month. Let us allow him 10 per cent for his leisure. We will even give him a holiday. That gives him approximately two bottles of Screech per month. That is what I am talking about.
This may seem a little funny to many hon. members, but I am talking about the average Newfoundland person who works in the average fishing operation and is trying to provide for his family delicious meals of the type for
10200	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers which we do not pay very much in the parliamentary restaurant. I should like to refer again to the average fisherman in Atlantic Canada, and I am glad to see the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) here tonight because he will well remember what I am going to say. Last year we had what everyone thought was a very good program by which the average fisherman was guaranteed-Mr. Speaker this is a word we really love, "guaranteed"-that he would receive for his fish the average of the price that he had received in the previous three years. This is what he was guaranteed last year. So he received between 2 cents and 4 cents per pound if he lived in Valleyfield, Newfoundland and as high as 4 cents a pound if he lived in the more affluent parts of the province. This was the guaranteed price for his fish. If you look at the prices of this type of product on the market it is difficult to believe what has happened.
Again this year, everyone was delighted to find that the same fisherman would receive the same price for his fish that he had received in the previous three years. Forget about the increase in the cost of living, the increase in taxation and the increase in educational costs, they were to be guaranteed the same price they received in the past three years. So, he received this year between 2 cents and 4 cents a pound and as high as 4 cents a pound for his fish. Look at the price per pound of fish in the supermarket. You would never believe it., I tell you that you will look twice before you purchase it. It is a little difficult to believe. I looked this weekend and a pound of fresh Atlantic cod was selling for 75 cents a pound and a pound of fresh haddock was selling for $1.25. Where is the money going? It is not going into the pockets of the fisherman because he is being literally so dehydrated economically that he will blow away. This is the situation with which we are faced. The money is not going into the pockets of the average Canadian fisherman. Something must be wrong. The minister sits there, but he spends $16 million. The department says, "Come to Poppa". We are coming to poppa, but poppa says he has no money. He has no power; he has nothing.
In this blue document I do not see one bit of evidence that anything is being done for the consumer. I see all kinds of people earning $16,000, $18,000, $20,000 or $35,000 working for the minister. There are all kinds of administrative costs. I should like to have hon. members look through this document. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace [Mr. Lundrigan.l
DEBATES	June 16, 1969
(Mr. Allmand) has left his seat but is still in the house. I say to him that he should glance through it and see where the money is going. I do not see any evidence there of anyone in this department working to help the consumer. The minister is building a $16 million empire for himself. I would like to have this $16 million. As I said before, the country would save $15 million and I would be a millionaire.
I could go on and talk about the cost of education. I went to university in 1956. I spent $720. I did not drink any beer. I did not smoke any cigarettes. I purchased my books I studied and spent $720. Two years later I spent $1,500. In 1965 I was a student again. It cost me and my family-this is not a good statistic-approximately $7,000. This year I doubt if the average Canadian student could get through university with less than about $2,000. But the same student cannot find a summer job. If he does find a job he cannot earn enough money to buy his books and pay his tuition. Four hundred and fifty dollars is about the cheapest tuition fee you can find at a Canadian university. Again, if he does happen to get this $450 he will end up having to obtain a student loan with the highest rate of interest. I could go on and tell the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that we do have a problem in Canada. Frankly speaking, I do not see any great effort being made by the government. You can present it in black, white, green, red, yellow, orange or in any way you like to show that we have a problem but they shake their heads. They do not see it.
Perhaps we have a government so geared to the sophisticated thinking about the great contributor to party funds that they cannot see beyond this. Basically, I do not think this government identifies itself with the average Canadian. I do not mind not being able to solve a problem overnight, but I do mind when we have a government which does not have in mind the interests of the average Canadian.

My only purpose in rising is to indicate that the basic producers, for the most part the farmers in this country, have not had an increase in the price of their raw materials in relation to the increases that have been charged at the retail level. I want to develop that point slightly, and then perhaps have one or two things to say about what has in fact happened over these a few years. The prices received by farmers for the products they sell, on the average have increased very little in recent years. In fact in 1951, 18 years ago, the index stood at 296.8 based on 1935-39 being 100. Of course we have to use that index because that is what was being used at that time. Last year, for the full year, the index was up to 302.2 on this base, or only up about 1 per cent. For the last month which is available, April, 1969, the D.B.S. indicates the index stood at 301, so it has gone up about 1 per cent on the average since 1951.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
The composite index relating to what was paid by farmers for the goods and services they need in order to carry on their operations, and this excludes their own living costs,
10201
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers rose by 70 per cent during that period. So when we contend that farmers have not received a justifiable increase in the prices of the products they sell on the market there are statistics to bear out this fact.
For example, there were some complaints about beef prices. On May 1, 1952, choice steers sold in Toronto at $25.26 per hundred weight or about 25J cents. That is not the highest point at which beef sold, but by May 1, 1952 beef prices had declined rather significantly from what they were a few weeks earlier.
Then, we turn to May 1, 1964, but I can give you the figures for 1963 or 1962 if hon. members think they would be happier figures because these were the years they were in office. I am not blaming them for the price of beef, but I am pointing out it had declined by May 1, 1964 to 24\ cents per pound. In May of 1966, the price stood at an average of 27i cents per pound for choice steers in Toronto. Bearing in mind these figures, sirloin steak sold on the market in 1952 for 93.4 cents per pound. There was a very small increase in receipts to farmers. By 1968, the price of sirloin steak had gone up to $1.26 per pound, with very little change in the live price of beef.
There has been a great deal of discussion about beef prices in the last few days, but this is not the only commodity for which there has been a price change. Let us turn to pork, for example. On May 1, 1952, a Grade A hog sold in Toronto at $26 per hundred pounds, and by 1968 this had gone up slightly to $27.55. Let us then take a look at the price of pork products being sold over the counter. On June 16, 1952 the price of pork products had increased. For example, pork chops were selling at 56.3 cents per pound. By 1968 this had gone up to 88 cents per pound and there had not been a significant change in the price received by the farmer.
You could go on and on to show this situation in respect of one commodity after the other. For instance, eggs were selling at 59.1 cents a dozen in 1952 and by 1968 the price had not even been maintained but had dropped to 55.6 cents.

That is the average price here in Canada.
The point I am trying to get at is there are some other inputs in the cost factor between the producer and the consumer who purchases at the retail level. To make a blanket

10202	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers condemnation of the government or anyone else involved in this situation, in my opinion, is not being honest, realistic or fair. There has been a very important change during that period of time in the kind of services that the consumer has demanded, and I mean demanded in a way that the consumer would be willing to pay for during this period of time. speechtext:
To further substantiate the point I am trying to make, I would like to quote some other statistics. In 1949 the farm value, or the farmer's receipt, as a per cent of the retail value on domestically produced foods- this includes the whole group-was about 60 per cent. By 1950 to 1954 his percentage of the dollar had gone down to 56 per cent; by 1955 to 1959 it had gone down to 47 per cent. Then there is the period that hon. members in the opposition like to talk about. I refer to the years 1960 to 1964. In that period, the percentage of the farm value of food had gone down from 47 per cent to 43 per cent. So, there was not any change just because a different government was in office. By 1965, the farm value was 44 per cent; by 1966 it had risen to 45 per cent; and in 1967 it went down to 43 per cent.
This has been going on regardless of change of government, and so on. It seems abundantly clear to me that when there are great complaints about the increase in the cost of living index and the component part related to food, this increase has not occurred because the farmer has obtained larger receipts. I notice that there are complaints about the cost of living and these complaints are usually made in regard to food; indeed, two or three years ago far more attention was paid to that component of the cost of living index than any other. Yet when you examine the facts, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures from 1950 to 1965 show that the price of food has increased less than any other component factor in the cost of living index. It is important that this be understood by the consumers of Canada.
I could go on for quite a long time and select other food items. I could go on and quote statistics to substantiate what I am trying to point out. However, I shall not do so because the opposition suddenly say they agree with me and have pointed out these things. We realize that there is an increase in the cost of food, but I suggest that when complaints are made that it is because of gross farm receipts, this is not the place to look for the increase in the cost of living.
I would also like to suggest that neither the opposition nor the people of Canada would like this or any other government to introduce rigid price controls. Price control in a free market economy is effected by what the
10203
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers consumer demands with her purchasing. There has been a very significant increase in the processing, packaging, servicing, and so on demanded by the Canadian consumer. I am not saying the Canadian consumer is wrong. If he or she wants it that way, of course all they need do is purchase highly processed foods. This has been going on for a long, long time.
The conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that if the situation with respect to beef is to be one in which the producer will be denied this recent adjustment in price, we will return to a situation where it is not profitable to produce these animals. I suggest that further down the road there will be more difficulty, because the supply situation will not meet the demand. This is precisely what has happened in the beef market during the last few weeks. What is more-and perhaps this is to some extent being overlooked-exactly the same thing is happening in the United States. Indeed, the increases we have experienced in this country were triggered in the United States some time in late March or April. So when we talk about a deficit supply of beef in relation to the demand, this is not confined to Canada; indeed, it is not even confined to North America. However, it did occur here rather suddenly. The unfortunate thing about this situation is that the price of beef did not start to move up and keep pace with the general price structure eight or ten years ago, If it had, we would not suddenly have found ourselves in the position we are today where there is an acute shortage in relation to the demand.
I hope all those people who may be inclined to condemn the farmer and the producer for the situation today will bear in mind all these other factors that are not only equally important, but are substantially more important in regard to what has happened to the price of some food products.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise with some hesitancy to speak in this debate, because I ask why I should make, in the eyes of the consumers, a knight in shining armour out of this so-called consumer affairs minister. He has attempted to gather consumers' votes all across Canada. It is a well known fact that there are more consumers than producers. It is a well known fact that there are more votes to be gathered by appeasing the consumer and asking: Who cares about the producer? The producer has become a very lowly force in the political sphere of Canada.

10204	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
One can readily see why the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Bas-ford), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) and the government have attempted to bring down the price of beef to the producer. In fact, since the minister's statement of two weeks ago one can check the statistics of the livestock market and he will find I am stating the fact. Two or three weeks ago in the Calgary market the price of prime steers to the producer was 35 cents a pound. Today it is down to 33 cents a pound. This is a direct result of the fear instilled by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs when he bought the argument of Loblaws which was quoted earlier today, and I shall quote it again. This newspaper article reads in part as follows:
Federal Consumer Affairs Minister Ron Basford has urged consumers to boycott beef, saying they are the only people who can bring the price down. His statements supported a boycott call by Leon Weinstein, President of the Loblaw Groceterias Ltd. supermarket chain.
The minister should put a feather in his hat because he has already brought down the price of beef to the producer by two cents a pound. I heard over the weekend the great defence of the primary producer by the Minister of Agriculture, who stated that the price of beef is justified. The producers have had no basic increase since 1951, when the price was as high as it is now. It took a sharp drop after 1951, and then slowly worked its way up again.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
I ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) : How are we going to keep up the price to the producer in view of the fact that his colleague in the cabinet is urging consumers to boycott beef? Is that the way the price is going to be maintained? I do not think he would agree with the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, and certainly no one in the primary producing field would agree. It is all well and good for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to agree with the grocery chains and the supermarkets, but what about the Batten report which was supported by the prairie provinces a few years ago? Who did the commissioners think was the biggest culprit responsible for the increased cost to the consumer? It was not the primary producer. They suspected it was the chain stores, and they had plenty of evidence to substantiate their suspicions. The minister said: Bring out your evidence, and a

DEBATES	June 16, 1969
member on the other side also asked for evidence. The Batten report brought forth plenty of evidence.
One can go back and look up the Gordon report of 1956 and 1957 in which the whole matter of the price of meat was dealt with. The minister sits there and chews his hearing aid. He would be better off if he put it in his ear and listened. It is all well and good for the Minister of Agriculture to suggest that, although he has come late to the defence of primary producers, better late than never. I suggest to him that he came to their aid two weeks late. What is the official position of his government with regard to the price of beef? That is the question that farmers ask themselves today. What did the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) have to say about this three weeks or a month ago in Vancouver? He said he urged primary producers in New Zealand and Australia to export beef to this country in the hope that it might lower the price of beef to Canadian consumers. How would it lower it, since it still has to go through the same marketing process and it still has to go through the same chain stores? It would lower the price of beef to the primary producer. That is who would be hurt.
There are two ministers over there against one. I think the one minister who is attempting to defend primary producers, instead of coming in two weeks late to their defence, in the future had better be two weeks early because he is against two ministers and it is pretty hard to predict where his leader stands in the matter. I would be inclined to think he is with the two rather than the one. In fact, there is no question about it. The price of beef has increased purely because of the shortage in the supply of beef, ever since the winter of 1964-65. One can go back and check the records to see that there has been a diminishing number of cows in the beef industry in Canada. At the same time the consumption of beef has gone up in the last 20 years, and so has the quality of the product. One has only to check the number of red and blue brands of beef that has been slaughtered every week over the past number of years to see that the percentage has gone up steadily every year. Consumers today are eating a better brand of beef. They are paying a little more for it, but it is nothing in comparison with the way in which the wage rates have increased.
Why has the number of cows gone down? Because farmers have not been able to foresee a return on the capital invested in the
June 16. 1969	COMMONS
ranching business which would warrant maintaining their cattle. That is the answer. Ranches have gone out of business and ranchers haven gone into other forms of the livestock industry. The Minister of Agriculture knows this well.
The same thing has been taking place in the United States, so that producers over there cannot ship cattle into this country because their prices are also high, as high as ours in any case. Prices here have gone up to where they should be. Now I ask: How are we going to keep them there, and how will we maintain this return? Members of this house know well the problems which agriculture faces today. The only phase of the agricultural industry that is not subsidized to any degree is the beef industry, and I defy the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs or anyone else in this house to stand up and say that this is not so. There may be an odd experimental farm or an odd grading or testing station here or there that is subsidized, but on the whole the beef industry is the only sector of agriculture that is not subsidized whatsoever. What is the government prepared to do in that regard? Hit it on the head and knock it down so that it has to be subsidized! This is the line of reasoning of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. I pity the Minister of Agrictulture whose defence of livestock producers is so weak. Surely, he can do better. Certainly he should do better.
I do not want to belabour the point this evening because in doing so I fear I will only aid the campaign which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has started. However, I must point out that agriculture today faces a severe crisis. There is wheat that has not been sold and there are feed grains that have not been sold. Our dairy products are subsidized to the tune of approximately $130 million a year, and yet surpluses are piled up in warehouses all across eastern Canada, particularly powdered skim milk. To top that off, the federal government has not assisted the farmers in marketing their products. On top of all that, most of southern Alberta and parts of Saskatchewan suffered a severe frost last week which brought untold damage once again to the agricultural industry. As if that was not enough, we now see the minister launch a campaign, with the aid of the C.B.C., to boycott the purchase of the one product which
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers the farmers produce without aid from the government.
I urge the Minister of Agriculture to consider how we are going to keep the price of beef at the level at which it should be. How will he convince the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs that the culprit may well be the chain stores which he so ardently supported? Is it because the Liberal party supports big money? Is it because big money has bought the Liberal party so that he has to support them in return in this hour of crisis for the agricultural industry? Is it because they have contributed a great deal toward the recent campaign of his lader? Is this why he feels that he has to support them and why he takes up their cause to protect them? The Batten report gives plenty of evidence as to why this situation has developed. Why does he not look into it? Is he afraid to find evidence that his own friends are the culprits and that the big money interests of the Liberal party are the culprits? Is this what he is afraid of?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
That is very interesting. I hope the minister carries this investigation to the limit in order to obtain the answer. As has been mentioned by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams), the price of beef to the consumer has gone up by approximately 68 cents a pound, which has brought a very small increase to the producer. Some of that increase has already tapered off as a result of the campaign which the minister started with the aid of the C.B.C. and the other news media.
I ask the Minister of Agriculture to take action in the defence of the primary producer and to do his fighting in the caucus. Let him condemn and educate his colleagues in the cabinet before they make any unwarranted charge against the only sector of the agricultural industry that is not a burden to the taxpayer today. Before they make any foolish statements again let him counsel them, advise them and urge them to seek advice from the people who know. These careless, offhand statements only reduce the price to the producer.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
There is one point the minister may have overlooked. When the producer received the lowest price for his product, the margin open to the chain stores goes up. This is documented in the Gordon report on our economic
10206	COMMONS
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers prospects, a report which came out in 1956 or 1957. When the primary producers receive least for meat on the hoof, whether hogs or cattle, the margin of profit open to the chain stores and processing plants widens, because there is a readiness on the part of consumers to buy. This is why the chain stores want the price of beef to the producer to drop; it is so they can get a bigger profit themselves. One has only to look at their profit figures to see that they have not suffered, The very fact that the numbers of cows has been so greatly reduced from 1954 onward suggests that farmers and ranchers have suffered, and have reduced their herds correspondingly. Once again I urge the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) to advise his cabinet colleagues so that they can make shrewder public statements, statements less injurious to the industry.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was surprised to see a fight developing between the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Basford) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext: What fight?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-FAILURE TO PROTECT CONSUMERS FROM ALLEGED EFFECTS OF INCREASING PRICES
speechtext:
It may be a paper fight. It certainly has not done any damage to the individuals concerned if they are carrying on a publicity campaign over the C.B.C. However, they have drummed up some interest in he subject and it may all be worthwhile. My view is that agricultural policy should be explained by the Minister of Agriculture to the minister of consumer affairs, because such policy has played a great role over the past few years in bringing about higher beef prices in Canada.
The minister referred to the year 1952. I remember that in those days we were producing milk. The milk went into a national pool where it was turned into large quantities of butter. The government's whole attention at that time was directed to the elimination of a butter surplus.
I recall that in those days we were selling day-old calves for $2. The other day I was surprised to learn from a person in the cow-calf operation that he had to get at least $100 from various sources as the price of that calf. Well, if the price of calves increases from $2 to $100 one can expect that the price of beef will be prohibitive. We have spent time and effort over a long period in getting rid of surpluses as they developed and part of our problem today lies in the nature of the short term measures used to get rid of those surpluses. Visiting dozens of farmers in the last 
DEBATES	June 16, 1969
few weeks, we have noticed an extreme shortage of calves for the feed industry. In future, the production of calves will become more and more difficult, partly because in western Canada the Liberal government has made plans to end what it calls the nonefficient production of cream.
Everyone raised on a farm knew that cream was uneconomic to produce. However, it is a by-product of the dairy industry. Many farmers were shipping one shotgun can of cream, but they were using the skim milk on the farm as a by-product to feed five or six calves.
All these calves went to the feeder cattle industry either directly or indirectly. We have cut this out. We have eliminated 30,000 or 40,000 of these producers who were so ineffective from the point of view of the government. I do not care what the minister of consumer affair does. Over the last ten years we have eliminated an important source of calf production in this country and we shall not be able to replace it. I think it is ridiculous for anyone to consider going into a cow-calf operation in circumstances where calves are worth $100. As I say, we used to sell these calves for $2 each. Indeed, only a few years ago I can remember going to auction sales and seeing day-old calves sold at from $15 to $25. Nowadays, there are not enough calves to meet the demand and prices will continue to increase.
The Department of Consumer Affairs will not be able to control this movement unless it is able to control the long term planning of the whole industry. Fortunately, here in Canada we have been able to produce food at low cost. We have not experienced the high field prices which have prevailed in other countries. We have always been able to produce in abundance. But if we make it uneconomic to operate any segment of agricultural production we shall be faced with shortages, and we may even be obliged to import food.
I listened to one of the speeches made this afternoon by an hon. member who was evidently using up some of the notes he had made for the budget debate. He told us this country had not done any worse than the United States. If the minister of consumer affairs is really interested in doing something for the consumers of this country he had better look at the attitudes his colleagues are taking toward the financial institutions of this country, because in every instance we have been discussing the problems of the agriculture industry we are finding that at the basis
June 16, 1969	COMMONS
of those problems lies the high rate of interest. Many of those who are engaged in the agriculture industry today are no longer farmers as I knew them or as the Minister of Agriculture knew them. They are agricultural-industrial producers and in most cases they are operating with at least $100,000 in capital, most of it borrowed at between eight or nine per cent. If they are to survive they will have to pay these rates and the only person who can enable them to do that is the consumer.
Any minister of consumer affairs worth his salt will have to consider methods of reducing the cost of capital or else we shall be in serious trouble. To return to the point I had begun to make earlier. The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. Allmand) said there was no problem-we were not much worse off than the United States. Possibly he has not looked at the financial pages reporting developments in the United States, but there is an indication that the United States may soon encounter yet more serious difficulties than those which face it at present. Apparently there is not sufficient money available to allow transactions to be made on the stock exchange-indications are that there may not be enough paper money to head off a run on the banks should a run develop. The hon. member may tell us we are no worse off than the United States but I can find little consolation in this assurance. The other day we talked to a number of farmers who were buying fertilizer, a most important commodity in all spheres of agricultural production.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
I was interested to note that farmers have to go to the United States to buy a new type of liquid fertilizer. It is not produced in the United States; this fertilizer is produced but a few miles from the farms of these farmers, yet it has to be bought in the United States from some source and delivered to them. This source was only a few miles away. Certain financial interests have now become involved and this liquid fertilizer is moved in bulk by trucks to the United States border. The bill of lading is then signed at the customs office, the fertilizer brought back into Canada and delivered to farms 15 to 20 miles away, I should like to know why this situation has not been referred to the combines investigation branch for investigation. These farmers were told this would be a waste of time. They were told that perhaps the United States might not sell them any fertilizer if they asked for an investigation. In the interest of reducing agricultural costs I think the minister would be
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers quite justified in spending some money in holding an investigation into such a situation. The farmers are told they will be penalized if an investigation is held, that consequently the investigation is not worth the effort.
There are many other commodities apart from fertilizer that might bear examination. I have read many reports by the combines investigation branch over the past three or four years and I agree with them that the penalties imposed are but a licence. A lot of money is being made from disgraceful monopolies of this sort. There is no effective combines legislation in this country. There is no protection from combines that increase the price of beef on the market.
A few minutes ago I noticed the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis) reading the back page of this evening's Ottawa newspaper, and if my memory serves me aright-though I did not pay too much attention-cheese is advertised at 56 cents a pound in Ottawa. Normally, this cheese sells in Ottawa stores for 78 cents, but apparently it has been put on special at 56 cents. The stores can do this because that cheese costs only 41 cents a pound in Belleville. The store would have to send the cheese from Ottawa to Belleville and pay for transportation both ways in order to store that cheese, so it is much better to sell it at 56 cents a pound and content yourself with 15 cents a pound on the transaction.
By selling that cheese at a fair market price of 56 cents a pound-and I suggest it could be sold a hell of a lot cheaper than that-we are helping the farmers in this area who produce cheese. We are also providing our consumers with a good protein diet at reasonable price. Why not investigate this situation and ascertain whether or not the mark up on Canadian Cheddar cheese is reasonable? I suggest a combine exists in the sale of cheese in which almost every dairy in the country participates. Only occasionally will a wholesaler put out a loss leader to a chain store, and this is to help the chainstore operator and does not show an interest in supplying a high protein product to the consumer.
It is my opinion that the consumer should not demand low cost agricultural products if this means the end of the industry. In my opinion we are not going to be able to reduce the price of beef to the consumer; rather the price will go up. It will go up because we have destroyed the cow-calf operation which is the basis of beef production. Without calves you cannot raise cattle for beef production. Western farmers can have as many bushels of
10208	COMMONS DEBATES	June 16. 1969
Failure to Reduce Prices to Consumers
gram as they want to give the cows, but unless you have a cow-calf operation you will not produce any beef from this source for the Canadian market.
It must be borne in mind that you cannot produce overnight a cow-calf operation; it is a long term project. This sort of operation was effectively destroyed when we decided to discontinue butter production from farm separated cream. I suggest the cabinet evolve some long term programs to deal with this problem and other problems, such as the present surplus of skim milk powder. I do not think we are going to change anything, but I do hope that the minister will consider the problem of combines that I have mentioned and the long term agricultural problems so that we can perhaps do something to remedy the situation before the consumers finds themselves unable to buy groceries.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize time is running out but may I have two or three minutes to debate this matter. I listened to the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Chappell), the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Kaplan) and the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace (Mr. All-mand) but I should like to comment first of all on something said by the hon. member for Don Valley. The hon. member said that as long as there are no signs of a depression or a recession, all is well. I do not understand that type of reasoning. After all, when the noose is tightening around one's throat one knows the end is very close. At such times you do not worry about whether or not there is going to be a depression or a recession.
I suggest that what is required is a policy to remedy what is a fact of life, namely a policy that will enable the people of Canada to buy what they cannot at the moment afford to buy. The hon. member for Don Valley must have thought that he was debating this question in front of some high school children, because he referred to economic theories and went on and on. The important thing to remember is that it is a fact of life that the cost of living is going up and up. Inflation is simply beyond comprehension.
I heard the hon. member for Peel South say that he was not even interested in the price of beef. Perhaps he is a vegetarian or is a consumer of caviar, but I should like to inform him that there are many people who are interested in the price of beef. These people want to know just what is going to happen to prices in this country; it is as simple as that.

The hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace dragged in the usual red herring and put many statistics on the record relating to the position in the United States.

Hon. members have somewhat embarrassed me, because I could carry on for some time now. Let me inform the hon. member for Notre-Dame-de-Grace that we are not interested in statistics in the United States or in Great Britain. What we want is some leadership from this government. The hon. member refers to the position in the United States of America, but that country has a gross national product that is five times ours and a population of 210 million. Let him not compare their economy with ours. If this government has any programs, we will carry them out. I was tickled when I saw the hon. member stand up to justify the minister's position. That is plural. One says, go ahead and block the increase in the price of beef. The other says he is happy about it. I would like to see members of the government get together now and again and come out with a statement on which they all agree. They say it does not matter. Nowadays frustration seems to be the point of this government- frustate the people, bring in the red herrings.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
It is very important that we debate items of this nature because I think the government is pulling the wool over the eyes of the Canadian people. Do you know what the government thinks is important? They think the official languages bill is important. I say one thing, if the bellies aren't full, you don't have to worry about any official languages bill. The government talks about the omnibus bill and homosexuality between two consenting adults. Who cares about that? Abortion? That may be important to some people, but those are the nitty-gritty issues. What is important are the nuts and bolts or bread and butter issues.

No, you cannot ask me a question. I have only four minutes. I wish to read a little story which will take up the balance of my time. This story is from the book, "Life for the Choosing", the 44th Annual Report, 1969, Board of Evangelism and Social Service, the United Church of Canada. The reference in this story is to poverty in Vancouver. I am even bringing in some one else's riding: I am reading from page 95.
When you're old and alone and you measure your days with nickels and dimes, rising prices are more than an inconvenience. They choke off life's last small pleasures and kill the final glimmer of hope for something better.
Mrs. McLeod was asked, how do you live on $1.54 a day? She replied, poorly. Now listen to this:
Old people, Mrs. McLeod rationalizes, have little need or yearning tor rich fare such as steaks, chops or roasts. She shops for bargains in liver, chicken wings, sausage; soup bones, at 10 or 15 cents each, are a staple.
That is almost what you would call soul food, Mr. Speaker.
"I make a lovely soup from two or three bones and some vegetables," she said. "I make enough for a week and put it in jam jars in my refrigerator. I have a jar of soup every day for my lunch."
What I want to know, Mr. Speaker, is whether or not the government is going to project the principles of the just society. The people of Canada are waiting for leadership. I say to the government, don't be hesitant to come before the people of Canada with ideas. I know the government is bankrupt of ideas. There is a crisis here that must be faced, Mr. Speaker. The people of Canada cannot stand the rising prices which we pay for meat, clothing, housing or rent. People need direction. This is the call of the government. This is why they have 155 seats, temporarily. Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to complete my remarks.

NOISE ABATEMENT-STEPS TO COMBAT NATIONAL PROBLEM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a few days ago on Orders of the Day I attempted to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro) a question relative to noise, and particularly noise in industry. I wanted to know what consideration the government is giving to this very important area of public health. Noise is now recognized as a major non-fatal disease in the United States, and last month that country took legislative action to combat it. At the time Mr. Speaker ruled the question out of order and, accordingly, I take advantage of this late period to raise it again.
Hon. members may recall that a few weeks earlier a bill of mine was given first reading, the point of which is to limit the noise

10210	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion volume in factories or other establishments having business with the Government of Canada to 85 decibels. I want to say at once that this limit of 85 decibels is a very high level and one which, in many minds, should be reduced to a much lower level. But in my opinion it would be a start and an example. At 85 decibels the noise volume is described by health experts as, "when you can hardly hear yourself speak." I am very hopeful that the Minister of National Health and Welfare who, in my opinion, is a very forward looking minister and is taking up the several health problems of the nation as best he can, will be interested in trying to do something about noise as a health factor as soon as his department can get around to it.
Hon. members may be familiar with recent magazine and newspaper agitation for action on this issue, I quote from an editorial in the Toronto Globe and Mail of May 26, which says in part:
How many of us escape . .. sound pollution? Even farmers, who are supposed to be safe in the quiet countryside are going deaf at a rattling rate because the tractors they drive make a racket from 7 to 29 decibels above the 85 decibel level at which hearing is damaged. Such hearing loss is imperceptible in its advance until it becomes serious, and it is incurable. Dr. Douglas Warren of the University of Toronto's School of Hygiene has described deafness, whether partial or total, as Canada's major non-killing public health problem. It is a sad condition, too, which often drives the victim into emotional isolation.
Yet this very serious problem has scarcely been assessed, let alone tackled.
I wish to give another brief quotation from a submission of the Ontario Federation of Labour, as follows:
The number of industrial workers subjected to harmful noises very likely exceeds those exposed to any other occupational hazard.
As I said earlier, last month the United States government moved to combat this health problem caused by noise. My question tonight is again, what action does the government, either through the Department of National Health and Welfare or the Department of Labour, intend to take to combat industrial unrest in Canada.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)

maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BOUNDARIES FOR WOOD BUFFALO PARK
NATIONAL PARKS-BOUNDARIES FOR WOOD BUFFALO PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my brief talk this evening arises as a result of a question I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) a few days ago. I do not know whether he is here or whether someone is here to answer for him. I saw him here a few moments ago. I asked him whether he could give some information concerning when negotiations with regard to the boundaries of Wood Buffalo park would be resumed between the province of Alberta and the federal government. I put this question to him because I feel the people of northeastern Alberta, Fort Chipewyan, Fort Smith and the people in part of northern Saskatchewan in the Eldorado region as well as the people in Fort McMurray, have been victimized by this government and to some extent perhaps by the government of the province of Alberta.
This victimizing has been done as a result of the two governments blaming each other for inactivity in respect of the development of Wood Buffalo park. There are two major problems which I should like to mention. One concerns the industrial development in the area of the park to provide jobs and the other is the matter of the construction of roads in the vicinity of the park in order to provide a communication link with the rest of the province. As I mentioned previously, the greatest problems in this region are those of isolation, unemployment and abject poverty among the
June 16, 1969
citizens who live in that section of the country.
In February, 1968 a northern roads conference was held at Fort McMurray at which representatives from the Alberta, Saskatchewan and the federal government participated. At that time these representatives from these three governments indicated that as soon as the federal government and the government of Alberta could reach some settlement concerning the boundaries of the park some sort of industrial development program would be undertaken.
When 1 came here last fall, I attempted to find out what negotiations, if any, were in fact going on. Much to my dismay I found that no active discussions had been going on for two years or more, and that the responses given to the people in that region brought about a misconception of the situation on their part. Prior to Christmas I asked the minister this question:
Are active negotiations under way between the federal and the Alberta governments concerning the Wood Buffalo Park boundaries and is an agreement imminent?
The answer was:
No, however, it is anticipated that discussions with the province of Alberta will be resumed in the near future. It is not possible to state when agreement will be reached at this time.
I spoke to the premier of the province of Alberta three weeks ago. At a public meeting he indicated that as soon as an agreement could be reached concerning where the boundaries should be they could proceed with some industrial development to provide jobs for the people of that area. I should like to know whether any negotiations are going on at the present time, whether the federal government has any plans to negotiate the ownership of that park, and if so when. The provincial government indicated it is willing to make a trade with the federal government for some land which I think is known as the "badlands". It is not willing to give as many acres of this land as are contained in Wood Buffalo Park, since this is such a huge area. The provincial government has at least led the people to believe that industrial development would take place in that region if that trade could be made and that development would be possible once it was no longer park land.
It is fair to say that the people in northeastern Alberta are tired of hearing one government blame another by saying that unless an agreement is reached nothing will happen 29180-6465
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion when there really is no intention that anything will happen. I was in Whitecourt a few weeks ago and the people there still think something is imminent and will happen within a few months or within the next year. I do not think anything will happen and it is not fair to the people in that area of the country to mislead them in this way.
There is to be a new road conference at Eldorado in the near future when people are supposed to be told about a new highway north of Fort McMurray to Fort Smith and Fort Chipewyan. The provincial government apparently has surveyed this highway and it will release information as to whether it will go ahead. I wonder whether the minister can tell us that the government really plans to participate in the construction of a highway like that. If he cannot, will he say so in order that the people will not expect something that is not going to happen? It is time we were honest with the people of Alberta, and I hope the minister can provide some of these answers.

speakerposition: Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
maintopic: NATIONAL PARKS-BOUNDARIES FOR WOOD BUFFALO PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for calling my attention to this problem of which I have been aware now for some time already.
It is true that in the Wood Buffalo Park, in Alberta, some problems now under consideration do exist.
The first matter which I should like to bring up is whether or not the Wood Buffalo National Park should be a provincial or federal park.
I must tell the hon. member that the land which was set aside for the Wood Buffalo National Park belonged to the federal government and that only later on was the control over that land passed on to the Alberta government. That land has always belonged to Her Majesty in the right of Canada and it is wrong to say that we should hand it back to the government of Alberta because it never belonged to it.
The Wood Buffalo National Park is a very big park. I know that problems do exist, that Indians are living there, and that it might be possible to work out some arrangements in order to meet their wishes and to promote their economic development. The problem exists and we are now studying plans related to it together with the government of Alberta.

10212	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
I must admit that negotiations may not be going as fast as the hon. member would wish, but in 1967 or 1968 I think my predecessor informed the government of Alberta that he was considering the possibility of some exchanges that might solve the problems now existing in the Wood Buffalo Park, which would enable us to complete our national parks network in Alberta by acquiring the undeveloped lands in the south of the province. However, the negotiations are still going on.
As for the problem of the road, I must say that it is a huge park and almost intact which constitutes one of the rare areas in Canada and even in America where such a large stretch of land has been reserved for the conservation of wild life. We have had some success with the conservation of the western buffaloes which represent a very important part of our national heritage.
I know that within 10, 15 or 20 years the people of Alberta like the other Canadians will be grateful to us for having taken the necessary measures to maintain this park in the best possible condition.
As for the question of building the road, it is connected with the importance of the park and with the activity that can be found there.
I know that the province is interested in building a road near the park and that some
DEBATES	June 16, 1969
border adjustments would perhaps be necessary so as to allow for its construction. I am prepared to discuss the matter with the government of Alberta in order to find a solution to this problem.
But I doubt that we have the necessary funds to build a road-unless the Alberta government wants to do it at its own expense-seeing the province can afford it; if it were to decide to do so, an agreement could certainly be reached-from the southern tip of the park to the Northwest Territories. Later on, it might be possible, but according to me, we would be unable to build it across the park within the next few years.
I can assure the hon. member that I take a personal interest in the problem, and that I shall take all the necessary steps to meet the demands of the people who live in the park, the Indians and, at the same time, to find an equitable solution not only for the citizens of Alberta but also for all those Canadians who are interested in conserving that land for future generations.
